name: Alice Guy Blaché
quote: There is nothing connected with the making of a film that a woman cannot do as easily as a man, being fully capable of mastering every technical detail of this art.

profile.content: Alice was born in Saint-Mandé in 1873. At age 6, Alice was sent to France to study at the Convent of the Sacred Heart, on the border with Switzerland, along with her siblings. After her father's death, Alice trained as a stenographer and typist, new fields at the time, in order to support her mother and herself. She got her first job at a varnish factory. A year later, in 1894, she began working with Léon Gaumont at the Comptoir général de la photographie.

In 1894, Alice was hired by Gaumont to work at the photography company as a secretary. The company soon collapsed, but Gaumont bought its inventory and started his own company, which would soon become a pioneering powerhouse of the French film industry. Alice decided to stay with Gaumont at his new company, the "Gaumont Film Company", a decision that would lead her to become a pioneer. On March 22, 1895, Alice and Gaumont attended the Lumières' surprise screening, where they showed one of the first films ever made, La Sortie de l'usine Lumière à Lyon.

In mid-1896, Alice released the world's first production with a cinematic narrative, La Fée aux choux (The Cabbage Fairy). From 1896 to 1906, she was head of production at Gaumont's studio and probably the only woman film director of that period. In 1906, she shot The Life of Christ, a large-scale production for its time, with three hundred extras.

In 1907, Alice married Herbert Blaché, who was soon put in charge of production for Gaumont's operations in the United States. After working with her husband in the United States, the two decided to set up their own company in 1910 with George A. Magie, thus creating the Solax Company, the largest film studio before Hollywood, with Alice being the first woman, or one of the first, to run a studio.

To focus solely on writing and directing, she handed the presidency of Solax over to Herbert. The couple tried to keep up a partnership for a while, but the relationship was short-lived. Herbert left his wife and children to try for a career in Hollywood with another actress.

Alice directed her last film in 1920, nearly dying of the flu during the production. On March 24, 1968, Alice died at the age of ninety-four while living in a nursing home.

name: Martin Scorsese
quote: As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster.

profile.content: Martin Scorsese was born in New York. He graduated from NYU's film school, drawing attention with short films such as It's Not Just You, Murray! (1964). He directed his first feature, I Call First (1967), was assistant director and co-editor of Woodstock (1970), and directed Boxcar Bertha (1972) for producer Roger Corman.

Launching one of the most acclaimed director-actor partnerships, Scorsese and Robert De Niro made Mean Streets, the first in a series of eight films. In 1980 came Raging Bull, a biography of boxer Jake La Motta, featuring lush black-and-white cinematography and a true tour de force performance by De Niro. Scorsese also made New York, New York (1977), a musical starring Liza Minnelli and De Niro, and The Last Waltz (1978), a film about the farewell concert of the group The Band.

The rest of the decade proved less receptive to Scorsese's originality. Although appreciated today, The King of Comedy (1982) was a failure. The Last Temptation of Christ (1988) received good reviews but was mired in controversy, sparking vehement protests from religious groups and being banned in some countries.

A reunion with De Niro produced the perfect mob film, Goodfellas (1990), a sinister remake of Cape Fear (1991), and Casino (1995). In 1990, the director created The Film Foundation, dedicated to film preservation. He directed the beautiful Kundun in 1997, a biography of the Dalai Lama.

Gangs of New York (2002) marked the beginning of a new collaboration with Leonardo DiCaprio, which would include The Aviator (2004) and The Departed (2006), the latter earning Scorsese a long-overdue Oscar. The Grammy-winning No Direction Home (2005) and Shine a Light (2008) continued his long involvement with the music documentary, celebrating the work of Bob Dylan and the Rolling Stones, respectively.

name: Georges Méliès
quote: He greets his audience as the dreamers and adventurers they truly are and invites them to dream along with him.

profile.content: Georges Méliès was born in 1861. He gained fame in Paris as an illusionist, founding the Théâtre Robert-Houdin.

Méliès began making films in the style of the Lumière brothers, but then discovered the camera's potential for illusion, essentially inventing special effects. His early films, just one reel long, were simple demonstrations of magic tricks such as transformations and disappearances.
He went on to make more complex films with multiple special-effects sequences linked by more elaborate plots. His last epics were seldom seen.
Bankrupt and out of filmmaking, Méliès was hailed as a master by the Surrealists and won national recognition: in 1931 he received the Legion of Honor.

name: Sergei Eisenstein
quote: The profession of film director can and should be so lofty and precious that no one may aspire to it while turning away from any knowledge that would make him a better director of films or a better human being.

profile.content: After a brief stint in the army, Sergei Eisenstein joined the theater in 1920. His first feature film was Strike (1925), followed the same year by Battleship Potemkin.

International recognition was key to Eisenstein obtaining permission to make October (1928), commemorating the 10th anniversary of the October Revolution. Charlie Chaplin (1889-1977) introduced him to the American writer Upton Sinclair, and together they began a project in Mexico that was never completed.

Eisenstein spent a period teaching and left a film, Bezhin Meadow (1937), unfinished, which led Stalin to view him with disfavor. After receiving a pardon, he returned with Alexander Nevsky (1938, see p. 142), a warning about the Nazi threat.

Ivan the Terrible, Part I (1944) was regarded as a portrait of the strength of the Russian people and their indomitable leader. In 1946, the director finished shooting the second part of this epic, but its depiction of leadership degenerating into tyranny enraged Stalin, and it was released only in 1958. Eisenstein suffered a heart attack while working on the third and final part of the film and died on February 11, 1948. The trilogy was never completed.

name: Buster Keaton
quote: A comedian does strange things. A good comedian does funny things.

profile.content: Joseph Frank Keaton was born on October 4, 1895. His family performed in vaudeville, and he made his stage debut in 1899.

Keaton appeared in his first film, The Butcher Boy (1917), opposite Fatty Arbuckle. His screen persona was already established, including his signature porkpie hat. His first leading role was in The Saphead (1920). Joseph M. Schenck found the young star so promising that he gave him his own production company, Buster Keaton Comedies.

This period was Keaton's golden age, in which his stone-faced character, daring sequences, and occasionally melancholic tone elevated his work above the studio comedies. Our Hospitality (1923) was followed by Sherlock Jr. and The Navigator (both 1924), College (1927), Steamboat Bill, Jr. and The Cameraman (both 1928). In all of his films, Keaton's characters are desperate to escape chaos and find solace in a simpler life.

Executives at MGM, Keaton's new studio, tried to rein in any excessive spending after the failure of The General. Ironically, his bland pairings with Jimmy Durante, especially What! No Beer? (1933), the last feature film starring Keaton, were among his biggest box-office hits.

In addition to a few notable cameos, including a guest appearance as a card player in Sunset Boulevard (1950), Keaton played small comic roles in a number of films, among them Around the World in 80 Days (1956) and It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World (1963). At 68, he starred in Film (1965), a 24-minute picture written by Samuel Beckett.
His last screen appearance was alongside Zero Mostel in A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, directed by Richard Lester (born 1932). Keaton died on February 1, 1966, in California.

name: Quentin Tarantino
quote: If you want to make a film, make it. Don't wait for funding, don't wait for perfect circumstances. Just make it.

profile.content: At 16, Quentin began studying acting at the James Best Theatre Company. At 22, he wrote his first screenplay, Captain Peachfuzz and the Anchovy Bandit. In 1984, Tarantino started working as a clerk at Video Archives.

He met Lawrence Bender at a party in Hollywood, who encouraged him to direct a film. The end result of that conversation was Reservoir Dogs. He turned down several projects, such as Speed and Men in Black, withdrew to Amsterdam, and began working on his screenplay for Pulp Fiction, which was released in 1994 and won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

After Pulp Fiction, he directed the fourth segment of the anthology Four Rooms, The Man from Hollywood, a remake of an episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents starring Steve McQueen. In 1997, he released his third film, Jackie Brown, a tribute to the blaxploitation genre. In 2003, he released Kill Bill, issued in two parts, Vol. 1 and Vol. 2, a project he created together with the film's lead actress, Uma Thurman, during the shooting of Pulp Fiction.

In partnership with Robert Rodriguez, Tarantino wrote and directed Death Proof, in addition to making guest appearances on American TV series. In 2009, he released one of his most acclaimed works, Inglourious Basterds, starring Brad Pitt, Christoph Waltz, Mélanie Laurent, and Diane Kruger. Four years later, he released Django Unchained, renewing his partnership with Christoph Waltz.

The Hateful Eight was released in 2015, shot in 70 mm and, for the first time, featuring an original score composed by Ennio Morricone, something the Italian had not done for a western in more than 34 years. Following the rape allegations against Harvey Weinstein in 2017, Tarantino released his newest film, Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, through Sony Pictures.

awards: Won 2 Oscars. Another 140 wins and 183 nominations.

name: Christopher Nolan
quote: Mankind was born on Earth, but it will not die here.

profile.content: After working on several short films, such as Tarantella, Larceny, and Doodlebug, he gained notoriety and caught the attention of the studios. In 1998, he released his first feature film, Following, and two years later, Memento (2000), acclaimed by critics who praised its unique nonlinear structure and its various themes, such as memory, perception, and revenge. In 2002, he released Insomnia, starring Al Pacino, Robin Williams, and Hilary Swank.

In early 2003, Nolan approached Warner Bros. with the idea of making a new Batman film. The film was released in 2005, with Christian Bale in the title role, alongside Michael Caine and Gary Oldman. After releasing his film The Prestige, Nolan released the second film of the Batman trilogy, The Dark Knight. Released in 2008 to immense critical acclaim, The Dark Knight has been regarded as one of the best films of the 2000s and one of the best superhero films of all time. At the 81st Academy Awards, it was nominated in eight categories, winning for "Best Sound Editing" and, posthumously, "Best Supporting Actor" for Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker.

In 2010, Nolan wrote and directed Inception, another critical and commercial success, before releasing the final film of the Batman trilogy, known as the "Dark Knight" trilogy: The Dark Knight Rises. In 2014, Interstellar, starring Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, Jessica Chastain, and Michael Caine, was released, receiving five Oscar nominations.

Nolan went on to serve as a producer on other Warner superhero films, such as Man of Steel and Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice. In 2017, he released Dunkirk, which received 5 Oscar nominations, one of them Nolan's first for Best Director.

awards: Nominated for 5 Oscars. Another 136 wins and 217 nominations.

name: Oscar Micheaux
quote: It is only by presenting those portions of the race portrayed in my pictures, in the light and background of their true state, that we can raise our people to greater heights.

profile.content: Oscar Devereaux Micheaux was born on a farm in Metropolis, Illinois, on January 2, 1884, the fifth of 13 children of a father who had been born enslaved in Kentucky. At 17, he went to Chicago, where he worked in stockyards, steel mills and at a shoeshine stand. He then became a porter on Pullman sleeping cars, a job that allowed him to save money and see the country. With his savings, he bought land in South Dakota and became a homesteader in a region where his neighbors were almost all white. The farm failed and was sold in 1911, but the experience would become raw material for his work.

media.title: Within Our Gates (1920)
media.text: The oldest surviving film directed by an African American faced protests and was banned in some theaters for showing a lynching.

profile.content: Before cinema, Micheaux was a writer. In 1913 he anonymously published the autobiographical novel The Conquest, and traveled the region selling his own books. In 1918, the Lincoln Motion Picture Company, a producer of Black filmmakers, wanted to adapt his novel The Homesteader, but refused to let him take part in the adaptation. Micheaux then created his own company, sold shares to investors and directed the film himself. Released in 1919 and now lost, The Homesteader (1919) is considered the first feature film directed by an African American and was a success with audiences and critics.

In 1920, Micheaux released Within Our Gates (1920), a drama about a teacher trying to save a school for Black children in the South that, in a long flashback, shows the lynching of her adoptive family. Released shortly after a wave of racial violence in the United States, the film was the target of protests and censorship. In Body and Soul (1925), Micheaux gave singer and actor Paul Robeson his first film role. His films, shown in theaters for Black audiences, the so-called race films, featured complex characters and tackled issues such as discrimination at work, violence and racism within the community itself.

media.title: Oscar Micheaux: the first independent Black filmmaker
media.text: A video summary of Micheaux's career, from homesteader in South Dakota to producer of more than 40 films.
media.source: YouTube: Black History in Two Minutes or so channel

profile.content: Micheaux made it through the arrival of sound and, in 1931, released The Exile (1931), the first talking feature produced by an African American. He worked on minimal budgets, shot quickly and personally distributed the prints, traveling from town to town. In all, he produced more than 40 films, but many have been lost. The Great Depression dried up his financing, and he returned to literature in the 1940s. He died in Charlotte, North Carolina, on March 25, 1951. His tombstone in Great Bend, Kansas, reads: "A man ahead of his time". In 2019, Body and Soul was added to the Library of Congress's National Film Registry.

media.quote: I am too imbued with the spirit of Booker T. Washington to engraft false virtues upon ourselves, to make ourselves that which we are not.
media.author: Oscar Micheaux, on his films

awards: Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame (1987) and a special award from the Directors Guild of America (DGA).

name: Charlie Chaplin
quote: Life is a tragedy when seen in close-up, but a comedy in long-shot.

profile.content: Charles Spencer Chaplin was born in London on April 16, 1889, the son of music hall performers. His childhood was marked by poverty: his father was absent, his mother struggled to support her children and Charlie was twice sent to a workhouse before he was nine. At 14, he saw his mother committed to a psychiatric hospital. He began performing as a boy, toured English theaters and, at 19, joined Fred Karno's troupe, which took him on tour to the United States. It was there that a representative of Keystone saw him on stage.

media.title: Modern Times (1936)
media.text: The Tramp swallowed by the gears of the factory: Chaplin's critique of automation and unemployment during the Great Depression.

profile.content: In 1914, Chaplin made his film debut at Mack Sennett's Keystone studios, and as early as Caught in the Rain (1914) he began directing his own films. The Tramp was born, with bowler hat, cane, baggy trousers and enormous shoes. At Essanay, in 1915, the character gained tenderness in The Tramp (1915), and the mix of slapstick and melancholy became his trademark. His fame exploded: the American press spoke of "Chaplinitis". In 1916, his contract with Mutual, worth US$ 670,000 a year, made him one of the best-paid men in the world, and shorts such as The Immigrant (1917) are still considered small masterpieces today.

In 1919, Chaplin founded the distributor United Artists with Douglas Fairbanks, Mary Pickford and D. W. Griffith, and gained full control over his films. The features followed: The Kid (1921), which blends comedy and drama in portraying the poor childhood he knew well; The Gold Rush (1925); and The Circus (1928), which earned him a special award at the first Oscar ceremony, in 1929. When sound arrived, Chaplin resisted. City Lights (1931) premiered in 1931 with virtually no dialogue, with music he composed himself, and closed with one of the most moving endings in cinema.

media.title: 1921: how Charlie Chaplin invented the "dramedy"
media.text: The One Hundred Years of Cinema channel shows how The Kid combined laughter and tears in the same story, something rare in the comedies of the time.
media.source: YouTube: One Hundred Years of Cinema channel

profile.content: Modern Times (1936) was the Tramp's farewell and a satire of factory life during the Great Depression. In The Great Dictator (1940), his first talking film, Chaplin ridiculed Adolf Hitler while the United States was not yet at war, and ended the film with a speech against fascism delivered straight to the camera. The 1940s, however, brought personal scandals, accusations of communist sympathies and an FBI investigation. In 1952, on his way to the premiere of Limelight (1952) in London, he had his re-entry permit to the United States revoked.

Chaplin decided not to return. He settled with his family in Corsier-sur-Vevey, Switzerland, from where he directed A King in New York (1957), a satire of McCarthyism, and A Countess from Hong Kong (1967), with Marlon Brando and Sophia Loren. In 1972, the Academy invited him to receive an honorary Oscar: it was his first visit to the United States in 20 years, and the audience gave him a standing ovation of about 12 minutes. The following year, he won the only competitive Oscar of his career, for the score of Limelight. He was knighted in 1975 and died on Christmas Day 1977, at age 88.

media.quote: More than machinery, we need humanity. More than cleverness, we need kindness and gentleness.
media.author: Charlie Chaplin in the final speech of The Great Dictator (1940)

awards: 2 honorary Oscars (1929 and 1972) and the Oscar for best original score for Limelight (1973).

name: Fritz Lang
quote: The mediator between the head and the hands must be the heart.

profile.content: Friedrich Christian Anton Lang was born in Vienna on December 5, 1890, the son of a master builder. He began studying civil engineering, but traded calculations for art: he traveled through Europe, Africa and Asia and studied painting in Paris in 1913. When World War I broke out, he enlisted in the Austrian army and fought in Russia and Romania. He was wounded four times and lost the sight of his right eye. While recovering, he began writing screenplays, his gateway to the film studios of Berlin, then the most inventive in Europe.

media.title: Metropolis (1927)
media.text: The vertical city of Metropolis: Lang's monumental sets and effects defined science fiction in cinema.

profile.content: In Berlin, Lang met the writer Thea von Harbou, whom he married in 1922 and who co-wrote all his films until 1933. The pair made Lang the leading name of Weimar Republic cinema: Der müde Tod (Destiny, 1921), the crime serial Dr. Mabuse, der Spieler (Dr. Mabuse, the Gambler, 1922), more than four hours long and divided into two parts, and the epic Die Nibelungen: Siegfried (1924). In 1927 came Metropolis (1927), UFA's most expensive production up to that time. The story of the futuristic city divided between the elite and the workers was a box-office failure on release, but its imagery still influences science fiction today.

After Spione (Spies, 1928) and Frau im Mond (Woman in the Moon, 1929), which invented the countdown before a rocket launch, Lang made his first talking film. M - Eine Stadt sucht einen Mörder (M, 1931) follows the hunt for a child murderer, played by Peter Lorre, pursued at the same time by the police and by Berlin's underworld. The use of sound is ingenious: the killer gives himself away by whistling a melody by Grieg. In 1933, with Hitler in power, the Nazi regime banned Das Testament des Dr. Mabuse (The Testament of Dr. Mabuse, 1933), in which the villain repeats phrases from party propaganda. Divorced from Thea von Harbou, who joined the Nazi party, Lang left Germany.

media.title: Why Metropolis still defines science fiction, 100 years later
media.text: A report by the German broadcaster DW on the making of the 1927 classic and its influence on cinema and pop culture.

profile.content: After a stay in Paris, Lang arrived in Hollywood in 1934 and became an American citizen in 1939. His first film in the United States, Fury (1936), confronts lynching and mass hysteria. Over two decades, he worked for several studios and helped shape film noir with its shadows, guilt and ordinary men dragged into crime: The Woman in the Window (1944), Scarlet Street (1945) and The Big Heat (1953) are examples. During the war, he made anti-Nazi films such as Hangmen Also Die! (1943), written with the playwright Bertolt Brecht.

Tired of conflicts with producers, Lang returned to West Germany in the late 1950s to shoot the two-part adventure Der Tiger von Eschnapur (The Tiger of Eschnapur, 1959) and Das indische Grabmal (The Indian Tomb, 1959), based on a story he had developed with Thea von Harbou in the 1920s. He ended his career as a director with Die 1000 Augen des Dr. Mabuse (The Thousand Eyes of Dr. Mabuse, 1960), returning to his most famous villain. In 1963, he played himself in Jean-Luc Godard's Le Mépris (Contempt, 1963), a tribute from the New Wave to the master. He died in Beverly Hills on August 2, 1976, at age 85.

media.quote: CinemaScope is not for men, but for snakes and funerals.
media.author: Fritz Lang playing himself in Contempt (1963)

awards: Commander's Cross of the Order of Merit of Germany (1957 and 1966); honorary professor of Fine Arts at the University of Vienna (1973).

name: Dorothy Arzner
quote: If one was going to be in this movie business, one should be a director, because he was the one who told everyone else what to do.

profile.content: Dorothy Emma Arzner was born in San Francisco on January 3, 1897, and grew up in Los Angeles, where her father ran a restaurant frequented by silent film stars such as Mary Pickford, Douglas Fairbanks and producer Mack Sennett. After high school, she spent two years studying medicine at the University of Southern California, because she wanted to be a doctor. During World War I, she enlisted in an ambulance service. When the war ended, the film industry in Los Angeles needed workers, and a college friend drove her to the door of the Paramount studio.

media.title: Dance, Girl, Dance (1940)
media.text: Maureen O'Hara and Lucille Ball as two dancer friends: Arzner's most studied film criticizes the male gaze on women's bodies.

profile.content: In 1919, Arzner started out typing scripts at Paramount to understand how films were made. Within six months, she became an editor at a studio subsidiary, where she cut 52 films. On Blood and Sand (1922), with Rudolph Valentino, she shot some of the bullfighting scenes without credit and intercut them with stock footage, saving the studio a fortune. The work caught the attention of director James Cruze, with whom she collaborated on several films. When she received an offer to direct at Columbia, she threatened to leave Paramount, which finally gave her a film.

Her debut, Fashions for Women (1927), was a box office hit, and Paramount entrusted her with its first talking picture, The Wild Party (1929), starring Clara Bow and Fredric March. So that the actress could move around despite the sound equipment, Arzner had the microphone attached to the end of a fishing rod, a solution cited as one of the origins of the boom mic. From 1927 until her retirement in 1943, she was the only woman directing features in Hollywood, apart from the veteran Lois Weber, and the first woman to join the Directors Guild.

media.title: Who was Dorothy Arzner?
media.text: The Australian museum ACMI sums up the career of the director who launched Katharine Hepburn, Rosalind Russell and Lucille Ball in film.
media.source: YouTube: ACMI – Australia's museum of screen culture channel

profile.content: Working freelance for several studios, Arzner made her best-known films: Christopher Strong (1933), with Katharine Hepburn as an aviator who falls in love with a married man; Craig's Wife (1936), with Rosalind Russell; and Dance, Girl, Dance (1940), with Lucille Ball and Maureen O'Hara, in which a dancer confronts the audience that watches her with contempt. Her films rejected female rivalry and gave women solidarity, ambition and desires of their own. After First Comes Courage (1943), she left Hollywood, for reasons that were never explained.

Arzner kept working with images: she made training films for the Women's Army Corps during World War II, directed Pepsi commercials at the invitation of her friend Joan Crawford and taught film in Pasadena and at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), where Francis Ford Coppola was one of her students. She lived for more than 40 years with choreographer Marion Morgan. Forgotten for decades, she was rediscovered by feminist critics in the 1970s and honored by the Directors Guild in 1975. She died in La Quinta, California, on October 1, 1979, at age 82.

media.quote: Isn't it wonderful that you've had such a great career, when you had no right to have a career at all?
media.author: Katharine Hepburn's telegram read at the tribute to Dorothy Arzner (1975)

awards: Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a tribute from the Directors Guild of America (1975).

name: Humberto Mauro
quote: Cinema is a waterfall.

profile.content: Humberto Duarte Mauro was born in Volta Grande, in the Zona da Mata region of Minas Gerais, on April 30, 1897, the son of a cultured, multilingual woman from Minas Gerais and an Italian immigrant. As a child, he moved with his family to Cataguases. He played the violin and the mandolin and was fascinated by mechanics: he started an engineering degree in Belo Horizonte, but dropped out to install electrical networks on the region's farms. He worked as an electrician in Rio de Janeiro and, back in Cataguases, married Maria Vilela de Almeida, known as Dona Bebê, in 1920. In 1923, he bought a still camera from Italian immigrant Pedro Comello and began to dream of cinema.

media.title: Ganga Bruta (1933)
media.text: Rejected on release, Humberto Mauro's drama was rediscovered in the 1950s and is now among the 100 best Brazilian films, according to Abraccine, the Brazilian film critics association.

profile.content: With Comello, Mauro founded the production company Phebo Sul America in Cataguases and, far from the big cities, created the most important regional cycle in Brazilian cinema, the Cataguases Cycle. An admirer of D. W. Griffith and King Vidor, he shot American-style adventures such as Tesouro Perdido (1927), awarded best Brazilian film of 1927. Then came Brasa Dormida (1928), which used the landscapes of Minas Gerais like few films of its time, and Sangue Mineiro (1929), considered his masterpiece of the period. Mauro had close ties with the town's young modernist poets, who published the magazine Revista Verde.

Invited by Adhemar Gonzaga, Mauro moved to Rio de Janeiro and made Lábios Sem Beijos (1930), one of the first films of Cinédia, then the most important studio in the country. There he shot Ganga Bruta (1933), with a daring narrative for its time, full of symbols and quick cuts, which earned him the nickname "Freud of Cascadura". The film was savaged on release in 1933 and only received due recognition decades later. For the production company Brasil Vita Filmes, owned by actress Carmen Santos, Mauro shot Favela dos Meus Amores (1935), with scenes filmed in a Rio favela and the participation of the Portela samba school.

media.title: Humberto Mauro and the Cataguases Cycle
media.text: The show Cinemascope reconstructs how an electrician from rural Minas Gerais turned Cataguases into a film hub in the 1920s.

profile.content: In 1936, at the invitation of Edgar Roquette-Pinto, Mauro joined the newly created National Institute of Educational Cinema (INCE), part of the Ministry of Education. In almost three decades, he directed more than 300 documentary shorts on science, health, history and popular culture. The Brasilianas series, which recorded folk songs and rural labor, is the best-remembered part of that output, and A Velha a Fiar (1964) became a classic of poetic documentary. During this period he made only three features, including O Descobrimento do Brasil (1937), with music by Heitor Villa-Lobos.

In his final years, Mauro became a reference for the Cinema Novo generation. Glauber Rocha and Nelson Pereira dos Santos declared themselves his admirers, and for Nelson he wrote the Tupi-language dialogue of How Tasty Was My Little Frenchman, awarded at the 1971 Brasília Film Festival. His last work was the short Carro de Bois (1974). Humberto Mauro died on November 5, 1983, in Volta Grande, at age 86. Today he is often remembered as the greatest Brazilian filmmaker of all time, and one of the cinemas of the Palácio das Artes, in Belo Horizonte, bears his name.

media.quote: In Ganga Bruta I wanted to see if I could create some Freudian effects, mainly through symbols.
media.author: Humberto Mauro on Ganga Bruta (1933)

awards: Saci Award for best director for O Canto da Saudade (1953); Candango for best dialogue for How Tasty Was My Little Frenchman (1971).

name: Alfred Hitchcock
quote: Drama is life with the dull bits cut out.

profile.content: Alfred Joseph Hitchcock was born on August 13, 1899, in Leytonstone, on the outskirts of London, the son of a greengrocer. He studied at a Jesuit school and took evening classes in engineering. He was working as an advertising draftsman at a telegraph cable company when he learned that Famous Players-Lasky, an arm of Paramount, was opening a studio in London. In 1919 he was hired to design the title cards of silent films and gradually became a screenwriter, art director and assistant director. In 1925, producer Michael Balcon gave him the chance to direct.

media.title: Vertigo (1958)
media.text: Kim Novak by the Golden Gate, in San Francisco: in 2012, the obsession of Vertigo knocked Citizen Kane off the top of Sight and Sound magazine's poll of the greatest film of all time.

profile.content: His first hit came with The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog (1927), the hunt for a Jack the Ripper-style killer, which already carried the theme that would haunt him all his life: the innocent man accused of a crime. In 1926, he married screenwriter and editor Alma Reville, his closest partner throughout his career. Blackmail (1929) was the first British talking picture, and in the 1930s Hitchcock became England's greatest director with spy thrillers such as The 39 Steps (1935) and The Lady Vanishes (1938). His success caught Hollywood's attention.

Hired by producer David O. Selznick, Hitchcock moved to the United States in 1939. His first American film, Rebecca (1940), won the Oscar for best picture. In the following years he perfected suspense: the audience knows more than the characters and suffers waiting for the bomb to go off. He made Shadow of a Doubt (1943), his own favorite, Notorious (1946), with Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman, and Rope (1948), edited to look like a single continuous shot. Starting with Strangers on a Train (1951), he strung together a series of hits that would make him the most famous director in the world.

media.title: How Hitchcock creates suspense
media.text: A video essay on the difference between surprise and suspense, the lesson Hitchcock repeated in interviews and applied in every scene.

profile.content: Between 1954 and 1960, Hitchcock made a run of masterpieces. Rear Window (1954) turns the viewer into a voyeur alongside James Stewart, confined to a wheelchair. Vertigo (1958) received a cold reception but today competes for the title of greatest film ever made. Then came North by Northwest (1959) and Psycho (1960), shot in black and white on a television budget and with the shower scene that changed horror. At the same time, Hitchcock hosted the TV series Alfred Hitchcock Presents (1955-1965), which made his profile one of the best-known images on the planet.

In The Birds (1963), ordinary birds become an unexplained threat. In 1962, Hitchcock gave the young French critic François Truffaut a long interview that became the book Hitchcock/Truffaut, decisive in getting him seen as an auteur and not just a craftsman of entertainment. He never won a competitive Oscar despite five nominations as director, but received the Irving G. Thalberg Award in 1968. His last film was Family Plot (1976). He was knighted in 1980 and died in Los Angeles on April 29 of that year, at age 80.

media.quote: There is no terror in the bang, only in the anticipation of it.
media.author: Alfred Hitchcock

awards: Irving G. Thalberg Award (1968), AFI Life Achievement Award (1979) and a knighthood (1980). Nominated 5 times for the Best Director Oscar.

name: Yasujirō Ozu
quote: I am like a tofu maker: I only know how to make tofu.

profile.content: Yasujirō Ozu was born in Tokyo on December 12, 1903, and spent much of his childhood away from his father, in the countryside, where he became a regular moviegoer and a fan of American films. A poor student who was thrown out of his school dormitory, he even worked as a substitute teacher at a school in the mountains. In 1923, with an uncle's help and against his father's wishes, he was hired by the Shochiku studio as a camera assistant. Three years later he became an assistant director and, according to studio legend, used a reprimand in the boss's office to pitch a screenplay.

media.title: Tokyo Story (1953)
media.text: An elderly couple visits their children in Tokyo and discovers they have no time for their parents: Ozu's most celebrated film.

profile.content: Ozu made his directing debut in 1927 with The Sword of Penitence, now lost, and spent the following years making short comedies and dramas about students and workers. In this period he was already using the low camera that would become his trademark. I Was Born, But... (1932), about two boys disappointed by their father's submission to his boss, is the masterpiece of his silent phase. Ozu was slow to embrace sound, which he only did in 1936. He was drafted by the Japanese army twice: he spent two years in China and, at the end of World War II, was stationed in Singapore, where he spent a year watching American films and was impressed by Citizen Kane.

Back in Japan, Ozu resumed his partnership with screenwriter Kogo Noda, who had written the script of his first film. The two measured the progress of their screenplays by the number of sake bottles they emptied. With actress Setsuko Hara, he made the so-called Noriko trilogy: Late Spring (1949), Early Summer (1951) and Tokyo Story (1953). These are simple stories about marriages, children leaving home and parents growing old, told with a static camera, almost always at the height of a person sitting on a tatami mat, and with shots of objects and landscapes separating the scenes. In 2012, Tokyo Story was voted the greatest film of all time by filmmakers in Sight and Sound magazine's poll.

media.title: Why did Ozu cut to a vase?
media.text: The Nerdwriter video essay analyzes the famous shots of objects and landscapes that interrupt the scenes in Ozu's films.

profile.content: In 1958, Ozu made his first color film, Equinox Flower (1958), and soon after remade one of his silent films as Floating Weeds (1959). Also in color came Good Morning (1959), Late Autumn (1960) and the last one, An Autumn Afternoon (1962). President of Japan's directors' association from 1955, he was the first filmmaker to receive the Japan Art Academy Prize, in 1959. He never married and lived with his mother until her death in 1961. A heavy smoker, he died of cancer on his 60th birthday, December 12, 1963.

Outside Japan, Ozu was only discovered after his death, when his films began to circulate at festivals and cinematheques in the 1960s and 1970s. Since then, he has influenced filmmakers as different as Wim Wenders, who made the documentary Tokyo-Ga in his honor, Hou Hsiao-hsien, Aki Kaurismäki and Hirokazu Kore-eda. His grave at the Engaku-ji temple in Kamakura, which he shares with his mother, bears no name: only the character mu, meaning "nothingness".

awards: Japan Art Academy Prize (1959), the first awarded to a filmmaker. Tokyo Story was voted the greatest film of all time by directors in the 2012 Sight and Sound poll.

name: Akira Kurosawa
quote: To be an artist means never to avert one's eyes.

profile.content: Akira Kurosawa was born in Tokyo on March 23, 1910, the youngest of eight children. He wanted to be a painter and attended an art school, but could not make a living from painting. His great influence was his older brother, Heigo, a silent film narrator in Tokyo's cinemas, who died in 1933. In 1936, Kurosawa answered an advertisement from the P.C.L. studio, which later became Toho, and was hired as an assistant director. His mentor was director Kajiro Yamamoto, who taught him that a good director must first master screenwriting.

media.title: Seven Samurai (1954)
media.text: Seven Samurai created the template of a team assembled for a mission, copied from The Magnificent Seven to countless action films.

profile.content: Kurosawa made his directing debut in the middle of the war with Sanshiro Sugata (1943), a popular hit. In Drunken Angel (1948), he began his partnership with actor Toshiro Mifune, who would star in 16 of his films. In 1951, Rashomon (1950), the story of a crime told in contradictory versions, surprisingly won the Golden Lion in Venice and received an honorary Oscar, opening the doors of the West to Japanese cinema. The following year he made Ikiru (1952), about a bureaucrat with cancer who decides to do something useful before he dies, one of his most humanist films.

Seven Samurai (1954) gave the action film an epic scale and influenced cinema all over the world. Kurosawa adapted Shakespeare to feudal Japan in Throne of Blood (1957), a version of Macbeth, and made The Hidden Fortress (1958), which George Lucas acknowledged as an inspiration for Star Wars. In 1960 he founded his own production company, which released Yojimbo (1961), remade without permission by Sergio Leone as A Fistful of Dollars. High and Low (1963) and Red Beard (1965), his last film with Mifune, closed the most productive phase of his career.

media.title: Akira Kurosawa, composing movement
media.text: The Every Frame a Painting channel shows how Kurosawa used wind, rain, extras and the camera to put movement into every shot.

profile.content: The following years were difficult. A Hollywood project fell through, Dodes'ka-den (1970), his first color film, flopped, and in 1971 Kurosawa attempted suicide. He recovered thanks to an invitation from the Soviet Union: Dersu Uzala (1975), shot in Siberia, won the Oscar for best foreign language film. American admirers George Lucas and Francis Ford Coppola helped finance Kagemusha (1980), winner of the Palme d'Or at Cannes. In 1985, at age 75, he released Ran (1985), a version of King Lear and the most expensive film in Japanese history up to that time.

In 1990, Kurosawa received an honorary Oscar presented by Lucas and Steven Spielberg and released Dreams (1990), a collection of episodes inspired by his own dreams, with Martin Scorsese as Vincent van Gogh. His last film was Madadayo (1993). He died in Tokyo on September 6, 1998, at age 88. His influence spans generations, from Sergio Leone and Sam Peckinpah to Lucas, Spielberg and Bong Joon-ho, and Stanley Kubrick called him one of the great directors of cinema.

media.quote: With a good script, a good director can make a masterpiece. With a bad script, even a good director can't make a good film.
media.author: Akira Kurosawa

awards: Golden Lion for Rashomon (1951), Palme d'Or for Kagemusha (1980), Foreign Language Film Oscar for Dersu Uzala (1976) and an honorary Oscar (1990).

name: Orson Welles
quote: A film is never really good unless the camera is an eye in the head of a poet.

profile.content: George Orson Welles was born on May 6, 1915, in Kenosha, Wisconsin. He lost his mother at nine and his father at 15 and was treated as a prodigy from an early age: he painted, acted and adapted Shakespeare while still at school. At 16, he made his acting debut at the Gate Theatre in Dublin, Ireland. Back in the United States, he directed plays for the Federal Theatre Project, such as a 1936 Macbeth staged with an all-Black cast, and in 1937 he founded the Mercury Theatre company with John Houseman, which would launch several actors of his films.

media.title: Citizen Kane (1941)
media.text: Deep focus, low cameras and visible ceilings: Welles's first film was voted the greatest of all time for decades.

profile.content: On October 30, 1938, the Mercury Theatre's radio adaptation of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds, broadcast as if it were a newscast, made Welles famous overnight. Hollywood chased him, and RKO offered him a contract with creative freedom unheard of for a newcomer. The result was Citizen Kane (1941), which he co-wrote with Herman J. Mankiewicz, produced, directed and starred in at age 25. Inspired by press magnate William Randolph Hearst, who tried to block its release, the film flopped at the box office but won the Oscar for screenplay and changed the language of cinema.

His second film, The Magnificent Ambersons (1942), was taken out of Welles's hands: while he was filming in Brazil, RKO cut almost 50 minutes and reshot the ending. The trip was part of It's All True, a project backed by the US government that recorded the Rio de Janeiro Carnival and the journey of four raft fishermen from Ceará. The studio canceled the film, which was never finished. From then on, Welles became known as an undisciplined genius and had to fight for financing on every project, such as The Stranger (1946) and The Lady from Shanghai (1947), whose final hall-of-mirrors scene is legendary.

media.title: 1941: Citizen Kane, what makes a masterpiece?
media.text: The One Hundred Years of Cinema channel explains the innovations of Citizen Kane in cinematography, sound and narrative structure.
media.source: YouTube: One Hundred Years of Cinema channel

profile.content: Welles moved to Europe and began funding his films with the money he earned as an actor, as in the role of Harry Lime in Carol Reed's The Third Man. His Othello (1951), shot piecemeal over several years, won the Grand Prix at the 1952 Cannes Film Festival. Back in Hollywood, he made Touch of Evil (1958), famous for its opening long take, and then shot in Europe Le Procès (The Trial, 1962), adapted from Kafka, and Campanadas a medianoche (Chimes at Midnight, 1965), about Shakespeare's Falstaff, which he considered his best work.

In 1971, Welles received an honorary Oscar and, in 1975, the American Film Institute's Life Achievement Award. One of his last films was the essay Vérités et Mensonges (F for Fake, 1973), about art forgers and about cinema itself as a conjuring trick. In his final years, he worked on several projects he could not finish. He died in Los Angeles on October 10, 1985, at age 70. His unfinished film The Other Side of the Wind (2018) was only completed in 2018, from the material he left behind.

media.quote: If you want a happy ending, that depends, of course, on where you stop your story.
media.author: Orson Welles

awards: Oscar for best original screenplay for Citizen Kane (1942), Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival for Othello (1952), an honorary Oscar (1971) and the AFI Life Achievement Award (1975).

name: Ingmar Bergman
quote: No art passes our conscience the way film does, going directly to our feelings, deep down into the dark rooms of our souls.

profile.content: Ernst Ingmar Bergman was born in Uppsala, Sweden, on July 14, 1918, the son of a nurse and a Lutheran minister who would later become chaplain to the King. His father was strict: Ingmar was locked in dark closets as punishment, and religion and guilt would fill his entire body of work. As a boy, he was given a magic lantern and a puppet theater, which he considered his most precious toys. In 1937 he entered Stockholm University to study art and literature, but spent most of his time in student theater and in movie theaters.

media.title: The Seventh Seal (1957)
media.text: The knight who plays chess with Death during the plague became one of the most famous and parodied images in film history.

profile.content: His first major work was the screenplay for Torment (1944), directed by Alf Sjöberg. Bergman made his directing debut in 1946 and alternated cinema with theater, which he directed all his life: in 1953 he took over the Malmö City Theatre, where he formed the group of actors who would accompany him for decades, including Max von Sydow, Bibi Andersson, Harriet Andersson and Gunnar Björnstrand. Sommaren med Monika (Summer with Monika, 1953) scandalized audiences with its sensuality, and Sommarnattens leende (Smiles of a Summer Night, 1955), awarded at Cannes in 1956, made his name known around the world.

In 1957, Bergman released two classics: Det sjunde inseglet (The Seventh Seal, 1957), a reflection on death and the silence of God in the Middle Ages, and Smultronstället (Wild Strawberries, 1957), an old professor's journey through his own memories, winner of the Golden Bear in Berlin. Then came Jungfrukällan (The Virgin Spring, 1960) and Såsom i en spegel (Through a Glass Darkly, 1961), which won him two consecutive foreign language film Oscars, and Nattvardsgästerna (Winter Light, 1963), about a pastor who has lost his faith. With cinematographer Sven Nykvist and the close-ups of his actresses' faces, he made Persona (1966), considered by many his masterpiece. Many films from this period were shot on the island of Fårö, which became his refuge.

media.title: Bergman unpublished: writing screenplays
media.text: An excerpt from the Ingmar Bergman Foundation archive in which the director talks about his writing process.

profile.content: In the 1970s, Bergman made Viskningar och rop (Cries and Whispers, 1972), a drama in red about three sisters facing death, and the miniseries Scener ur ett äktenskap (Scenes from a Marriage, 1974), with Liv Ullmann and Erland Josephson, a devastating portrait of a marriage. In 1976, he was arrested during a rehearsal at the Royal Dramatic Theatre and charged with tax evasion. The charges were dropped, but, humiliated, he went into exile in Munich, Germany. Back in Sweden, he shot Fanny och Alexander (Fanny and Alexander, 1982), a family saga that won four Oscars, including best foreign language film, and which he announced as his farewell to cinema.

Bergman kept directing plays, operas and films for television, and wrote screenplays directed by others, such as Bille August's The Best Intentions, winner of the Palme d'Or in 1992. He published his autobiography, The Magic Lantern, in 1987. His last work was Saraband (2003), made for television with the characters of Scenes from a Marriage. He died in his sleep at his home on Fårö on July 30, 2007, at age 89, on the same day that Italian director Michelangelo Antonioni died.

media.quote: Probably the greatest film artist, all things considered, since the invention of the motion picture camera.
media.author: Woody Allen on Ingmar Bergman

awards: 3 Oscars for best foreign language film (The Virgin Spring, Through a Glass Darkly and Fanny and Alexander), the Irving G. Thalberg Award (1971), the Golden Bear for Wild Strawberries (1958) and the Palme des Palmes at Cannes (1997).

name: Federico Fellini
quote: There is no end. There is no beginning. There is only the infinite passion of life.

profile.content: Federico Fellini was born in Rimini, on the Adriatic coast, on January 20, 1920, the son of a traveling salesman. As a child, he drew, staged puppet shows and was fascinated by the circus and comics. In 1939 he moved to Rome, where he became a caricaturist and writer for the humor magazine Marc'Aurelio and began writing sketches for radio and gags for films. It was on the radio that he met actress Giulietta Masina, whom he married in 1943 and who would be his partner and muse for the rest of his life.

media.title: La Dolce Vita (1960)
media.text: Marcello Mastroianni and Anita Ekberg in the Trevi Fountain: the most famous scene of the film that gave the world the word "paparazzi".

profile.content: After the war, Fellini joined neorealism: he was one of the screenwriters of Roberto Rossellini's Rome, Open City (1945), which earned him his first Oscar nomination. He made his directing debut in 1950, alongside Alberto Lattuada, and soon found his own path with Lo sceicco bianco (The White Sheik, 1952) and I vitelloni (1953), winner of the Silver Lion in Venice. With Masina as the naive Gelsomina, La strada (1954) won the first competitive Oscar for best foreign language film in history. She would return as a dreamy prostitute in Le notti di Cabiria (Nights of Cabiria, 1957), another Oscar winner.

With Marcello Mastroianni as a journalist adrift in Roman high society, La dolce vita (1960) broke box office records, scandalized the Church and won the Palme d'Or at Cannes. The photographer Paparazzo, one of the characters, gave his name to celebrity photographers. Next, Fellini made 8½ (1963), about a director in crisis who can't get his next film started, with Mastroianni as his alter ego. Between memories, fantasies and the music of Nino Rota, his partner on almost all his films, it is one of the most influential films about the act of creation itself.

media.title: La Strada, trailer for the restored version
media.text: Giulietta Masina, Anthony Quinn and Richard Basehart in the circus road movie that gave Fellini his first Oscar.

profile.content: The following films plunged fully into the director's private universe, notable for its excess, its unusual faces and the sets built in Studio 5 at Cinecittà, his favorite studio. Giulietta degli spiriti (Juliet of the Spirits, 1965) was his first color film, followed by the ancient Rome of Fellini – satyricon (Satyricon, 1969). In Amarcord (1973), Fellini recreated the Rimini of his youth under fascism, with memories, caricatures and great tenderness, and won his fourth Oscar for best foreign language film, a record to this day.

In his final years, Fellini made films such as E la nave va (1983) and Ginger and Fred (1986), in which he reunited Masina and Mastroianni in a satire of television, and ended his career with The Voice of the Moon (1990). In March 1993, he received an honorary Oscar for lifetime achievement, at a ceremony in which Masina cried in the audience. He died in Rome on October 31 of that year, at age 73, one day after their 50th wedding anniversary. Giulietta died five months later. The adjective "Felliniesque" became a synonym for extravagant and dreamlike.

media.quote: Talking about dreams is like talking about movies, since the cinema uses the language of dreams.
media.author: Federico Fellini

awards: 4 Oscars for best foreign language film (La Strada, Nights of Cabiria, 8½ and Amarcord), an honorary Oscar (1993) and the Palme d'Or for La Dolce Vita (1960).

name: Satyajit Ray
quote: It is, without any doubt, the best achievement of my movie-making career.

profile.content: Satyajit Ray was born in Calcutta on May 2, 1921, into a family of Bengali artists and intellectuals. His grandfather founded a children's magazine, and his father, the poet Sukumar Ray, died when his son was two. Satyajit studied economics in Calcutta and, at his mother's insistence, art at the Santiniketan university founded by the poet Rabindranath Tagore. In 1943 he went to work as an illustrator at a British advertising agency and, among other jobs, illustrated an edition of the novel Pather Panchali. In 1949, he met Jean Renoir, who was filming The River in India, and the Frenchman encouraged him to make films.

media.title: Pather Panchali (1955)
media.text: Apu and his sister Durga discover the world in a Bengal village: shot with amateur actors and little money, the film became a landmark of world cinema.

profile.content: In 1950, the agency sent Ray to London, where he saw 99 films in six months. The one that struck him most was Vittorio De Sica's Bicycle Thieves: on his return, he decided to shoot Pather Panchali the same way, with amateur actors and real locations. With no producers interested, he started shooting at the end of 1952 with his own savings and spent two and a half years filming bit by bit, until he obtained the money to finish from the West Bengal government. Pather Panchali (1955) premiered in 1955 and, the following year, won the "Best Human Document" award at Cannes.

The story of the boy Apu continued in Aparajito (1956), winner of the Golden Lion in Venice, and ended in The World of Apu (1959), forming the Apu Trilogy, one of the great works of cinema. In the same period, Ray made The Music Room (1958), about a ruined aristocrat who spends what is left of his fortune on music concerts, and launched actors such as Soumitra Chatterjee and Sharmila Tagore. In 1964 came Charulata (1964), adapted from Tagore, about a lonely wife in 19th-century Calcutta, the film he himself considered his favorite.

media.title: How Satyajit Ray directs a film
media.text: The StudioBinder channel analyzes the realism, natural light and music of Ray's films, whose scores he also composed.

profile.content: Ray was a complete artist: he wrote, composed the scores, designed posters and costumes and created characters of children's literature who are still popular in India today, such as the detective Feluda and the scientist Professor Shonku. In cinema, he ranged through musical fantasy, comedy, history and politics, with the so-called Calcutta trilogy, about young people in the city in the 1970s. In 1977, he made his first Hindustani-language feature, The Chess Players, about the annexation of an Indian kingdom by the British.

In 1983, while shooting The Home and the World, Ray suffered a heart attack that greatly limited his work from then on; his son, Sandip, began operating the camera for him. His last film was The Stranger (1991). In 1992, he became the first Indian to receive an honorary Oscar. Already in hospital in serious condition, he received the statuette via a video link, from the hands of Audrey Hepburn, and gave his thanks from his hospital bed. That same year, he received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honor. He died in Calcutta on April 23, 1992, at age 70, leaving 36 films including features, shorts and documentaries.

media.quote: Not to have seen the cinema of Ray means existing in the world without seeing the sun or the moon.
media.author: Akira Kurosawa on Satyajit Ray

awards: Honorary Oscar (1992), Bharat Ratna (1992), the Golden Lion for Aparajito (1957) and the "Best Human Document" award at Cannes for Pather Panchali (1956).

name: Ousmane Sembène
quote: Cinema is the people's night school.

profile.content: Ousmane Sembène was born in Ziguinchor, in the Casamance region of southern Senegal, then a French colony, on January 1, 1923, the son of a fisherman. He studied at a Quranic school and at a French school, which he left in 1936 after a clash with the principal. He fished with his father until he was 15, when he moved to Dakar and lived off manual labor. In 1944, during World War II, he was drafted into the Tirailleurs Sénégalais, the colonial troops of the French army, and later served with the Free French Forces. The experience of fighting for a colonial power that treated Africans as second-class citizens would mark his entire body of work.

media.title: Black Girl (1966)
media.text: A young Senegalese woman works as a maid for a French family in Antibes: the first feature by a director from sub-Saharan Africa.

profile.content: At the end of 1947, Sembène stowed away to France. He worked at a Citroën factory in Paris and then as a docker in the port of Marseille, where he joined the trade union movement. Self-taught, he improved his French on his own and made his debut as a writer with The Black Docker (1956). His most famous novel, Les Bouts de Bois de Dieu (God's Bits of Wood, 1960), about the strike of the Dakar-Niger railway workers, made him one of the great names of African literature. But Sembène realized that books did not reach most of his people, who did not read French.

At almost 40, Sembène went to study film for a year at the Gorky studios in Moscow. Back in Senegal, independent since 1960, he shot the short Borom sarret (1963), about a cart driver in Dakar. In 1966, La Noire de... (Black Girl, 1966) became the first feature film released by a director from sub-Saharan Africa and won the Prix Jean Vigo in France. With Mandabi (1968), he fulfilled his dream of filming in Wolof, the most widely spoken language in the country. In Xala (1975), adapted from his own novel, he satirized the new African elite that took the place of the colonizers.

media.title: Ousmane Sembène on cinema as activism
media.text: In this excerpt released by Criterion, the director explains why he switched from literature to cinema to reach African audiences.

profile.content: Sembène never shied away from confrontation. Ceddo (1978), about a people's resistance to forced conversion to Islam in Africa centuries ago, had scenes cut by the Senegalese government, and he responded by handing out leaflets in cinemas describing what had been censored. Camp de Thiaroye (1988) reconstructed the massacre of African soldiers by the French army in 1944. His last film, Moolaadé (2004), about women who refuse to subject their daughters to genital mutilation, won awards at Cannes and at the African festival Fespaco. He died in Dakar on June 9, 2007, at age 84, called "the father of African cinema".

awards: Prix Jean Vigo for Black Girl (1966) and the Un Certain Regard prize at Cannes for Moolaadé (2004). He is considered the father of African cinema.

name: Agnès Varda
quote: If we opened people up, we'd find landscapes. If we opened me up, we'd find beaches.

profile.content: Arlette Varda was born in Ixelles, Belgium, on May 30, 1928, the daughter of a Frenchwoman and an engineer from a Greek family. In 1940, fleeing the war, the family moved to Sète, in the south of France, where they lived on a boat. Agnès, as she came to call herself, studied art history at the Louvre and then photography, and went to work as a photographer for the Théâtre National Populaire in Paris. She herself said she knew little about cinema and had seen very few films when she decided, at 26, to film the fishing village of Sète.

media.title: Cléo from 5 to 7 (1962)
media.text: A singer awaits the result of a medical test while wandering through Paris, almost in real time: Varda's portrait of fear and of how others look at us.

profile.content: Made with no experience and her own money, La Pointe Courte (1955), edited by Alain Resnais, is considered a precursor of the French New Wave, which would only emerge four years later. In 1962, Varda released Cléo de 5 à 7 (Cléo from 5 to 7, 1962), which follows almost in real time two hours in the life of a singer awaiting a diagnosis. That same year, she married filmmaker Jacques Demy, director of The Umbrellas of Cherbourg. With Le Bonheur (Happiness, 1965), a disturbing love story in vibrant colors, she won the Silver Bear in Berlin.

In the late 1960s, Varda lived with Demy in Los Angeles, where she shot a short film about the Black Panthers. Back in France, she made films about women's lives, such as One Sings, the Other Doesn't (1977), about the fight for abortion rights. In Sans toit ni loi (Vagabond, 1985), Sandrine Bonnaire plays a young drifter found dead in winter, whose story is told by those who crossed her path. The film won the Golden Lion in Venice in 1985. After Demy's death in 1990, she made Jacquot de Nantes, about her husband's childhood.

media.title: Through Agnès Varda's looking glass
media.text: The Nerdwriter channel analyzes how Varda mixed documentary, fiction and her own presence in front of the camera.

profile.content: With a small digital camera, Varda reinvented the documentary in Les Glaneurs et la Glaneuse (The Gleaners and I, 2000), about people who live off what is left from harvests and city garbage. In The Beaches of Agnès (2008), she told her own life story, and in Visages Villages (Faces Places, 2017), co-directed with the artist JR, she traveled through rural France pasting giant portraits of workers on walls; the film was nominated for an Oscar. The first woman to receive an honorary Palme d'Or, in 2015, and the first female director to receive an honorary Oscar, in 2017, she said goodbye with Varda by Agnès, screened in Berlin. She died in Paris on March 29, 2019, at age 90.

awards: Golden Lion for Vagabond (1985), Silver Bear for Happiness (1965), an honorary Palme d'Or (2015) and an honorary Oscar (2017), the first given to a female director.

name: Stanley Kubrick
quote: If it can be written, or thought, it can be filmed.

profile.content: Stanley Kubrick was born in New York on July 26, 1928, the son of a doctor. He was a mediocre student but passionate about chess and photography, which he learned with a camera given to him by his father. At 17, he sold a photo to Look magazine, which hired him as a photographer. In the following years, he frequented the screenings at the Museum of Modern Art and New York's movie theaters. With his savings, in 1951 he made the documentary short Day of the Fight (1951), about boxer Walter Cartier, whom he had photographed for the magazine. He sold the film, quit his job and decided to become a filmmaker.

media.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)
media.text: The effects of 2001, made years before computer graphics, still impress and gave Kubrick the only Oscar of his career.

profile.content: After two features made almost single-handedly, Fear and Desire (1953) and Killer's Kiss (1955), Kubrick met producer James B. Harris while playing chess in Washington Square and made with him The Killing (1956), a heist told across several timelines. With Kirk Douglas, he shot Paths of Glory (1957), about French soldiers executed for cowardice in World War I, and took over the direction of the epic Spartacus (1960), his only experience without full control of a film. In 1962 he adapted Vladimir Nabokov's Lolita (1962) and moved to England, where he would live for the rest of his life.

From the 1960s on, each Kubrick film was an event. Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb (1964) turned the fear of nuclear war into a black comedy, with Peter Sellers in three roles. 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), written with science fiction author Arthur C. Clarke, took years to make and changed space films forever. A Clockwork Orange (1971) caused so much controversy in England that the director himself withdrew the film from release there. In Barry Lyndon (1975), he shot scenes by candlelight with lenses developed for NASA, as if they were 18th-century paintings.

media.title: Why we're obsessed with Kubrick's films
media.text: The StudioBinder channel analyzes the symmetry, long takes, music and rigor that made Kubrick's style unmistakable.

profile.content: Reclusive in his home in England, Kubrick released films at ever-longer intervals. The Shining (1980), adapted from Stephen King, used the newly invented Steadicam to follow a boy on a tricycle through the corridors of an empty hotel. Full Metal Jacket (1987) showed boot camp and the Vietnam War, and Eyes Wide Shut (1999), with Tom Cruise and Nicole Kidman, was shot over more than a year. Kubrick died in his sleep of a heart attack on March 7, 1999, at age 70, six days after screening the final cut for his family and the actors. His project A.I. was completed by Steven Spielberg in 2001.

media.quote: I tried to create a visual experience, one that bypasses verbalized pigeonholing and directly penetrates the subconscious with an emotional and philosophic content.
media.author: Stanley Kubrick on 2001, in an interview with Playboy (1968)

awards: Oscar for visual effects for 2001: A Space Odyssey (1969), the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement (1997) and the Directors Guild's D. W. Griffith Award (1997).

name: Jean-Luc Godard
quote: Photography is truth. The cinema is truth 24 times per second.

profile.content: Jean-Luc Godard was born in Paris on December 3, 1930, into a wealthy Protestant family of French-Swiss origin: his father was a doctor and his mother came from a family of bankers. He spent part of his childhood and youth in Switzerland. In Paris, in the late 1940s, he frequented film clubs and the Cinémathèque Française, where he met François Truffaut, Jacques Rivette and Éric Rohmer. As a critic for Cahiers du Cinéma, he attacked traditional French cinema, championed American directors such as Alfred Hitchcock and Howard Hawks and began making his first short films.

media.title: Breathless (1960)
media.text: Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg on the streets of Paris: handheld camera, natural light and cuts that jump in time.

profile.content: From a story by Truffaut, Godard shot À bout de souffle (Breathless, 1960) in 1959, with a handheld camera, natural light and the famous jump cuts within the same scene. The film became a manifesto of the French New Wave. A decade of dizzying output followed, often with actress Anna Karina, whom he married in 1961: Vivre sa vie: film en douze tableaux (Vivre Sa Vie, 1962), Bande à part (Band of Outsiders, 1964) and Pierrot le fou (1965). He also made Le Mépris (Contempt, 1963), with Brigitte Bardot, and Alphaville, une étrange aventure de Lemmy Caution (Alphaville, 1965), science fiction shot in the Paris of the time, which won the Golden Bear in Berlin. His films mixed genres, quotations, posters and reflections on consumer society.

After La Chinoise (1967) and Week End (1967), Godard radicalized. In May 1968, alongside Truffaut, he led the protests that shut down the Cannes Film Festival in solidarity with students and workers. In the following years, he abandoned commercial cinema and created the Dziga Vertov Group with Jean-Pierre Gorin, which made low-budget militant films. In the late 1970s, he moved to Switzerland and began working with filmmaker Anne-Marie Miéville, his partner for the rest of his life, experimenting with video and television.

media.title: Breathless: how World War II changed cinema
media.text: The Nerdwriter video essay shows where the freedom and the cuts of Breathless came from and why the film seemed so new in 1960.

profile.content: Godard returned to theaters in the 1980s with films such as Every Man for Himself and First Name: Carmen, winner of the Golden Lion in Venice in 1983. For a decade, he edited the video series Histoire(s) du Cinéma, a reflection on the 20th century through films. He refused to go to Los Angeles to receive his 2010 honorary Oscar. At 83, he made Adieu au langage (Goodbye to Language, 2014), in 3D, winner of the jury prize at Cannes, and at 87 he received a special Palme d'Or. He died on September 13, 2022, at age 91, in Rolle, Switzerland, by assisted suicide, which is legal in the country.

media.quote: A film should have a beginning, a middle and an end, but not necessarily in that order.
media.author: Jean-Luc Godard

awards: Golden Bear for Alphaville (1965), Silver Bear for best director for Breathless (1960), the Golden Lion for First Name: Carmen (1983), an honorary Oscar (2010) and a special Palme d'Or (2018).

name: Andrei Tarkovsky
quote: The artist exists because the world is not perfect.

profile.content: Andrei Arsenyevich Tarkovsky was born on April 4, 1932, in the village of Zavrazhye, about 500 kilometers from Moscow, the son of the poet Arseny Tarkovsky. His father left the family when he was small, and his childhood during World War II, with his mother and grandmother, would become material for his films. He studied Arabic at the Oriental Institute in Moscow, dropped out and spent a year on a prospecting expedition in the Siberian taiga, where he decided to study film. In 1954, he entered the State Institute of Cinematography (VGIK) in Moscow, where he studied under director Mikhail Romm and met Andrei Konchalovsky, his screenwriting partner.

media.title: Stalker (1979)
media.text: The Zone in Stalker, a forbidden territory where wishes can come true: Tarkovsky's last film in the Soviet Union.

profile.content: His first feature, Ivan's Childhood (1962), about a boy who serves as a spy in World War II, won the Golden Lion in Venice in 1962. Next came Andrei Rublev (1966), about the 15th-century Russian icon painter. The black-and-white epic was shelved by Soviet censors for five years because of its violence, nudity and religious vision, and only reached the West when it was screened at Cannes in 1969. At home, Tarkovsky came to be seen as a difficult and expensive auteur, always at odds with the state studio Mosfilm.

Solaris (1972), adapted from the novel by Polish writer Stanisław Lem, was presented as a Soviet answer to 2001: A Space Odyssey, but it traded technology for memory and guilt, and won the Grand Prix of the Jury at Cannes. In Mirror (1975), Tarkovsky assembled an autobiographical puzzle of childhood memories, archival footage and his father's poems. After a troubled shoot, he released Stalker (1979), inspired by the book by the Strugatsky brothers, in which a guide leads two men to a forbidden area where wishes come true.

media.title: A message from Andrei Tarkovsky to young people
media.text: In the documentary Directed by Andrei Tarkovsky, the director talks about solitude, time and the value of the inner life.

profile.content: Tarkovsky went to Italy to shoot Nostalgia (Nostalghia, 1983), about a Russian writer who cannot adapt to life abroad, which won the Best Director award at Cannes in 1983, shared with Robert Bresson. In 1984, he announced that he would not return to the Soviet Union. His last film, Offret (The Sacrifice, 1986), was shot in Sweden with Ingmar Bergman's crew, including cinematographer Sven Nykvist. Already ill with cancer, he could not go to Cannes to receive the Grand Prix of the Jury. He died near Paris on December 29, 1986, at age 54. His book Sculpting in Time is required reading for filmmakers.

media.quote: Tarkovsky for me is the greatest, the one who invented a new language, true to the nature of film, as it captures life as a reflection, life as a dream.
media.author: Ingmar Bergman in the book The Magic Lantern (1987)

awards: Golden Lion for Ivan's Childhood (1962), Grand Prix of the Jury at Cannes for Solaris (1972) and The Sacrifice (1986) and the Best Director award at Cannes for Nostalghia (1983), shared with Robert Bresson.

name: Francis Ford Coppola
quote: My film is not about Vietnam. It is Vietnam.

profile.content: Francis Ford Coppola was born in Detroit on April 7, 1939, the son of flutist and composer Carmine Coppola, and grew up in New York in a family of Italian descent. As a child, he had polio and spent long periods in bed, putting on puppet shows and playing with projectors. He studied theater at Hofstra University and film at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). He started out working for B-movie producer Roger Corman, who let him direct the horror film Dementia 13 (1963) with the leftover budget of another film shot in Ireland.

media.title: The Godfather (1972)
media.text: Marlon Brando as Vito Corleone: the film that saved Paramount and still tops lists of the greatest of all time.

profile.content: In 1969, Coppola founded the production company American Zoetrope with George Lucas in San Francisco, to make films away from the major studios. In 1971, he won the Oscar for screenplay for Patton, written with Edmund H. North. Paramount chose him, after several other directors had turned it down, to adapt Mario Puzo's mafia novel. Coppola fought for the casting of Marlon Brando and the then little-known Al Pacino and was nearly fired during the shoot. The Godfather (1972) was a resounding success and won the Oscars for best picture and adapted screenplay.

In 1974, Coppola released two films that rank among the best of the decade. The Conversation (1974), about a surveillance expert tormented by guilt, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes. The Godfather Part II (1974), which alternates Michael Corleone's rise with the youth of Vito, played by Robert De Niro, was the first sequel to win the Oscar for best picture and earned Coppola the award for best director. Then came Apocalypse Now (1979), a shoot of more than a year in the Philippines, with a typhoon, a heart attack suffered by the lead actor and a blown budget. The result won the Palme d'Or in 1979.

media.title: Francis Ford Coppola breaks down his most iconic films
media.text: In an interview with GQ magazine, the director recalls the making of The Godfather, The Conversation and Apocalypse Now.

profile.content: The musical One from the Heart (1982), shot entirely in the studio, flopped and left Zoetrope buried in debt. To pay off the debts, Coppola directed commissioned films in the 1980s and 1990s, but he also made The Outsiders (1983) and Rumble Fish (1983), which launched a generation of young actors, and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1992), made only with practical and in-camera effects. In 1990, he closed the trilogy with The Godfather Part III (1990). At the same time, he built a successful wine business in California. His daughter, Sofia Coppola, also became a director and won the Oscar for screenplay for Lost in Translation.

After small, personal films such as Tetro (2009), Coppola devoted himself to the project he had cherished for decades. Megalopolis (2024), a fable about the rebuilding of a decaying New York, was funded with about US$ 120 million out of his own pocket and premiered in competition at Cannes in 2024, dividing critics. That same year he was honored by the Kennedy Center and, in April 2025, he received the American Film Institute's Life Achievement Award. Even past 85, he keeps announcing new projects.

media.quote: What Francis does, creatively, is jump off cliffs. When you spend enough time with him, you start to believe you can jump too.
media.author: George Lucas at the Kennedy Center tribute to Coppola (2024)

awards: 5 Oscars (including best picture, director and screenplay for The Godfather Part II), 2 Palmes d'Or (The Conversation and Apocalypse Now) and the AFI Life Achievement Award (2025).
