name: Glauber Rocha
quote: A camera in your hand and an idea in your head.

profile.content: Glauber Pedro de Andrade Rocha was born in Vitória da Conquista, in the backlands of Bahia, Brazil, on March 14, 1939. In 1947, the family moved to Salvador, where he studied at a Presbyterian school and soon got involved with theater, radio, film clubs and the student movement. At 20, he shot the experimental short Pátio (1959) with leftover negative from another film. He entered the Bahia Law School but dropped out in 1961 to work as a journalist and film critic, always championing a Brazilian cinema that would break with the Hollywood model.

media.title: Black God, White Devil (1964)
media.text: Othon Bastos as the cangaceiro Corisco: Glauber's sertão blended folk ballads, westerns and opera.

profile.content: In 1962, Glauber made his feature debut with Barravento (The Turning Wind, 1962), about a fishing community in Bahia, awarded at the Karlovy Vary festival. Two years later came Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol (Black God, White Devil, 1964), the saga of the cowherd Manuel, who wanders the sertão between a messianic holy man and the cangaceiro Corisco, hunted by the hired killer Antônio das Mortes. Screened at Cannes, the film made Glauber the leading name of Cinema Novo, alongside Nelson Pereira dos Santos and Cacá Diegues. In 1965, he wrote the manifesto An Aesthetic of Hunger, which advocated a cinema made with few resources to show the poverty of the Third World without exoticism.

Made after the 1964 military coup, Terra em Transe (Entranced Earth, 1967) is an allegory about an imaginary country, Eldorado, where a poet wavers between populist and conservative politicians. The film won the FIPRESCI Prize at Cannes and became one of the fiercest portraits of Latin American politics. Next, Glauber made his first color film, O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro (Antonio das Mortes, 1969), which brought back Antônio das Mortes and won him the Best Director award at Cannes in 1969, with the support of the jury president, Luchino Visconti. As the dictatorship tightened its grip, he began filming abroad.

media.title: What was Cinema Novo?
media.text: An overview of the movement Glauber led in the 1960s, from Rio, 40 Graus to Entranced Earth.

profile.content: Persecuted by the military regime, Glauber went into exile in 1971 and passed through Cuba, Portugal, Italy, France and other countries, where he shot films such as Der Leone Have Sept Cabeças (The Lion Has Seven Heads, 1971), in Congo, and Claro, in Rome. He returned to Brazil in 1976 and shot the controversial short Di-Glauber, about the wake of the painter Di Cavalcanti, awarded at Cannes. His last film, A Idade da Terra (The Age of the Earth, 1980), was screened in Venice in 1980, where Glauber protested against the festival's results. Ill, he was living in Sintra, Portugal, when he was rushed back to Rio de Janeiro, where he died on August 22, 1981, at age 42.

media.quote: The most noble cultural manifestation of hunger is violence.
media.author: Glauber Rocha in the manifesto An Aesthetic of Hunger (1965)

profile.content: Glauber left a body of work that still divides and fascinates. In 2015, he became the director with the most films on the Brazilian Film Critics Association's list of the 100 best Brazilian films of all time, with five titles. In 2014, documents released by the National Truth Commission showed that the military regime monitored his interviews abroad. Cine Guarani, in Salvador, where he premiered several of his films, was renamed Cine Glauber Rocha, and his children Eryk Rocha and Ava Rocha went on to careers in film and music.

awards: Best Director award at Cannes for Antonio das Mortes (1969), the FIPRESCI Prize at Cannes for Entranced Earth (1967) and the Special Jury Prize at Cannes for Di-Glauber (1977).

name: Abbas Kiarostami
quote: I believe in an unfinished cinema, which is completed by the creative spirit of the audience.

profile.content: Abbas Kiarostami was born in Tehran on June 22, 1940. His first passion was painting: at 18, he won a competition and soon afterward left home to study painting and graphic design at the Faculty of Fine Arts of the University of Tehran. In the 1960s, he worked in advertising, designed posters, illustrated children's books and, between 1962 and 1966, shot about 150 commercials for Iranian television. The experience with short, precise images made on little money would be a school for the cinema he would make later.

media.title: Taste of Cherry (1997)
media.text: A man drives through the hills of Tehran looking for someone willing to bury him: the film gave Iran its first Palme d'Or.

profile.content: In 1970, Kiarostami helped set up the film department of the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults, known as Kanoon, in Tehran, and made his debut there with the short The Bread and Alley, about a boy and a dog. For two decades, he made films for and about children. Unlike many of his colleagues, he stayed in Iran after the 1979 Islamic Revolution. With Where Is The Friend's House? (1987), about a boy who crosses villages to return a classmate's notebook, he gained international attention and began the so-called Koker trilogy, named after the village where the film takes place.

Close-Up (1990) blends documentary and reenactment to tell the true story of a man who impersonated filmmaker Mohsen Makhmalbaf, with the people involved playing themselves. After the 1990 earthquake that devastated the Koker region, Kiarostami returned there in Life, and Nothing More… (1992) and Through the Olive Trees (1994). In 1997, Taste of Cherry (1997) won the Palme d'Or at Cannes. Two years later, The Wind Will Carry Us (1999) received the Grand Jury Prize in Venice. His long takes inside cars, zigzagging roads and open endings became a trademark.

media.title: The minimalist cinema of Abbas Kiarostami
media.text: A video essay on the apparent simplicity of Kiarostami's films and the viewer's role in completing them.

profile.content: In the 2000s, Kiarostami experimented with digital cameras in films such as Ten, shot entirely inside a car, and Shirin, made only of the faces of actresses watching a film. He was also a poet and photographer. Later, he filmed outside Iran: Copie conforme (Certified Copy, 2010), in Italy, won Juliette Binoche the best actress award at Cannes, and Like Someone in Love (2012) was shot in Japan. Ill since early 2016, when he underwent surgery on his digestive tract, he died in Paris on July 4 of that year, at age 76. His last work, 24 Frames, made from 24 of his photographs, was released in 2017.

media.quote: Film begins with D. W. Griffith and ends with Abbas Kiarostami.
media.author: Jean-Luc Godard

awards: Palme d'Or for Taste of Cherry (1997), the Grand Jury Prize in Venice for The Wind Will Carry Us (1999) and the Roberto Rossellini Prize (1992).

name: Hayao Miyazaki
quote: Once you've met someone you never really forget them. It just takes a while for your memories to return.

profile.content: Hayao Miyazaki was born in Tokyo on January 5, 1941, the second of four brothers. His father ran the family factory, which made parts for Japanese fighter planes in World War II, and that is where his passion for flying machines came from. Some of his earliest memories are of bombed cities. His mother spent years bedridden with tuberculosis, an experience he would recreate in My Neighbor Totoro. With a degree in political science and economics, he joined Toei Animation in 1963, where he began his long partnership with director Isao Takahata, with whom he worked on TV series for more than a decade.

media.title: Spirited Away (2001)
media.text: Chihiro in the spirit world: the film won the Golden Bear and the Oscar and was Japan's highest-grossing film for almost 20 years.

profile.content: Miyazaki made his feature debut with The Castle of Cagliostro (1979), an adventure of the thief Lupin. At the same time, he was publishing the manga Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, whose success gave rise to the film Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984), about a princess who tries to reconcile humans with a contaminated nature. The following year, he founded Studio Ghibli with Takahata and producer Toshio Suzuki. Then came Castle in the Sky (1986) and My Neighbor Totoro (1988), whose forest spirit became the studio's mascot and one of the most beloved characters in Japanese animation.

With Kiki's Delivery Service (1989) and Porco Rosso (1992), about a pilot turned into a pig in the Mediterranean of the 1930s, Miyazaki consolidated recurring themes: brave girls, a fascination with flight, pacifism and respect for nature. Princess Mononoke (1997), an epic about the war between humans and the gods of the forest, broke records in Japan. In 2001, Spirited Away (2001) became the highest-grossing film in the country's history, a record that lasted almost two decades, and won the Golden Bear in Berlin and the Oscar for animated feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony, in protest against the Iraq War.

media.title: How Studio Ghibli makes animation feel alive
media.text: The kaptainkristian channel shows the small gestures, pauses and everyday details that bring Miyazaki's films to life.

profile.content: Miyazaki kept drawing by hand in Howl's Moving Castle (2004) and Ponyo (2008). In 2013, after The Wind Rises (2013), about the engineer who designed the Zero fighter, he announced his retirement, and the following year he received an honorary Oscar. But he did not stop: he quietly began working on The Boy and the Heron (2023), released in 2023, which earned him his second Oscar for animated feature at age 83, the oldest director to win in the category. In 2016, upon seeing an animation made by artificial intelligence, he called it "an insult to life itself", a phrase that resurfaced as these tools became popular.

awards: 2 Oscars for animated feature (Spirited Away and The Boy and the Heron), the Golden Bear for Spirited Away (2002), an honorary Oscar (2014) and the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement (2005).

name: Steven Spielberg
quote: I dream for a living.

profile.content: Steven Allan Spielberg was born in Cincinnati on December 18, 1946, the son of a computer engineer and a pianist. He grew up in New Jersey and Arizona, where, as a teenager, he made amateur films with the family camera and charged the neighbors admission. His parents' divorce, which would mark several of his films, happened when he was young. After a tour of the Universal studios, he began hanging around the lot without permission. A short film, Amblin' (1968), earned him a seven-year contract with the studio, which put him to work directing episodes of TV series.

media.title: Jaws (1975)
media.text: The mechanical shark kept breaking down, so Spielberg decided to show it as little as possible: the thriller became the first summer blockbuster.

profile.content: The TV movie Duel (1971), about a driver chased by a truck on a deserted road, caught the critics' attention. After The Sugarland Express (1974), his first theatrical film, Spielberg took on Jaws (1975). The shoot at sea blew through its schedule and budget, but the film became the highest-grossing in history up to that time and invented the summer blockbuster model, released in hundreds of theaters at once. Next came Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977), which turned contact with extraterrestrials into an almost religious experience, with the score by John Williams, his partner on almost all his films.

With George Lucas, Spielberg created Indiana Jones in Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981), a tribute to the adventure serials the two had watched as children. E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982), about a lonely boy who hides an alien, broke the record of Star Wars and became the highest-grossing film in history. Through Amblin, the production company he founded in 1981, he also produced hits such as Back to the Future and Gremlins. At the same time, he pursued more adult films, such as The Color Purple (1985) and Empire of the Sun (1987), received with suspicion by some critics.

media.title: The Spielberg oner
media.text: The Every Frame a Painting channel shows how Spielberg films long scenes without cuts that almost nobody notices.

profile.content: In 1993, Spielberg released two films that show both sides of his work. Jurassic Park (1993) reinvented visual effects with digital dinosaurs, and Schindler's List (1993), in black and white, about the businessman who saved more than a thousand Jews from the Holocaust, won him the Oscars for best picture and director. With the profits, he created the Shoah Foundation, which recorded tens of thousands of survivor testimonies. In 1994, he founded the DreamWorks studio. Saving Private Ryan (1998), with its recreation of D-Day, won him his second Oscar for best director. He also made Minority Report (2002) and Catch Me If You Can (2002).

Spielberg kept alternating adventures, such as The Adventures of Tintin (2011) and Ready Player One (2018), with historical dramas, such as Lincoln (2012) and Bridge of Spies (2015). In 2021, he made his version of the musical West Side Story (2021) and, the following year, told the story of his own childhood in The Fabelmans (2022), winner of the People's Choice Award in Toronto and nominated for seven Oscars. In June 2026, he returned to flying saucers with Disclosure Day (2026), an original UFO film written by David Koepp from an idea of his, with Emily Blunt and Josh O'Connor in the cast.

awards: 3 Oscars (best picture and director for Schindler's List and director for Saving Private Ryan), the Irving G. Thalberg Award (1987) and the Presidential Medal of Freedom (2015).

name: Pedro Almodóvar
quote: When I put a clip from a film into mine, it's not a homage, it's outright theft.

profile.content: Pedro Almodóvar Caballero was born on September 25, 1949, in Calzada de Calatrava, a small rural town in the La Mancha region of Spain. At eight, he was sent to a religious school in Cáceres, because his family hoped he would become a priest. In 1967, against his parents' wishes, he moved to Madrid to make films, but Francisco Franco's dictatorship closed the city's official film school, and he taught himself. To support himself, he worked for 12 years at the phone company Telefónica and, with his first salary, bought a Super 8 camera to shoot shorts, while acting in avant-garde theater groups.

media.title: All About My Mother (1999)
media.text: Cecilia Roth as a mother who loses her son and goes to Barcelona in search of the past: the film won Almodóvar Best Director at Cannes and the Oscar.

profile.content: After Franco's death in 1975, Madrid lived through the Movida, an explosion of sexual, artistic and political freedom, and Almodóvar became the filmmaker of that moment. His first feature, Pepi, Luci, Bom y otras chicas del montón (Pepi, Luci, Bom, 1980), is a symbol of the era. Outrageous comedies followed, full of color, nuns, drugs and LGBTQIA+ characters, such as ¿Qué he hecho yo para merecer esto? (What Have I Done to Deserve This?, 1984). In 1986, he founded the production company El Deseo with his brother, Agustín. International success came with Mujeres al borde de un ataque de nervios (Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, 1988), with Carmen Maura, nominated for the Oscar for best foreign language film and a box-office hit in the United States.

In the 1990s, Almodóvar gradually traded provocation for mature melodrama, without losing his humor or his taste for kitsch. Carne trémula (Live Flesh, 1997) marked his first work with Penélope Cruz, his great collaborator alongside Antonio Banderas. Then came his most celebrated works: Todo sobre mi madre (All About My Mother, 1999), dedicated to actresses and mothers, which won him Best Director at Cannes and the Oscar for best foreign language film, and Hable con ella (Talk to Her, 2002), about two men who care for women in comas, which earned him the Oscar for best original screenplay.

media.title: Total design: Almodóvar's colors and sets
media.text: A MUBI video essay on the look of Law of Desire and Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, where every object has a dramatic function.

profile.content: In Volver (2006), Almodóvar returned to his native La Mancha with a story of three generations of women, and the entire female cast shared the best actress award at Cannes. Then came the thriller La piel que habito (The Skin I Live In, 2011), with Banderas as an obsessed surgeon, and Julieta (2016), adapted from the writer Alice Munro. In Dolor y gloria (Pain and Glory, 2019), he made his most autobiographical film: Banderas plays an aging director, with aches in his body and unable to write, who remembers his childhood and his mother, played by Penélope Cruz.

During the pandemic, Almodóvar directed the English-language shorts The Human Voice (2020) and Extraña forma de vida (Strange Way of Life, 2023), and the drama Madres paralelas (Parallel Mothers, 2021), which won Penélope Cruz the Volpi Cup in Venice. His first English-language feature, La habitación de al lado (The Room Next Door, 2024), with Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore, won the 2024 Golden Lion, the first for a Spanish film. In 2026, he returned to Spanish with Amarga Navidad (Bitter Christmas, 2026), which premiered at the Cannes Film Festival. The adjective "Almodóvarian" became a synonym for his universe of saturated colors, boleros and strong women.

awards: Oscar for best original screenplay for Talk to Her (2003), the Oscar for best foreign language film for All About My Mother (2000), Best Director at Cannes (1999) and the Golden Lion for The Room Next Door (2024).

name: Jane Campion
quote: What a death! What a chance! What a surprise! My will has chosen life!

profile.content: Elizabeth Jane Campion was born in Wellington, New Zealand, on April 30, 1954. Her parents, an actress and writer and a theater and opera director, founded one of the country's first professional theater companies, and she grew up backstage. Even so, she initially rejected an artistic career: she graduated in anthropology in 1975. She then studied art in London and painting in Sydney, Australia, until she entered the Australian Film, Television and Radio School. Her first short, Peel (1982), about a family arguing by the side of the road, would win the Short Film Palme d'Or in 1986.

media.title: The Piano (1993)
media.text: Holly Hunter as Ada, a mute woman who arrives in 19th-century New Zealand with her daughter and a piano: the film won Campion the Palme d'Or.

profile.content: After a few award-winning shorts and a TV movie, Campion made her feature debut with Sweetie (1989), a strange and funny portrait of two sisters that competed for the Palme d'Or at Cannes. Next she made An Angel at My Table (1990), a biopic of New Zealand writer Janet Frame, who spent years in psychiatric hospitals after a mistaken diagnosis of schizophrenia. Originally made as a TV miniseries, the film won the Grand Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival and drew the world's attention to the director.

The Piano (1993), with Holly Hunter, Harvey Keitel, Sam Neill and the young Anna Paquin, made Campion the first woman to win the Palme d'Or at Cannes, shared with Farewell My Concubine. The film also won her the Oscar for best original screenplay, and she became the second woman nominated for the Oscar for best director. Then came The Portrait of a Lady (1996), adapted from Henry James, In the Cut (2003) and Bright Star (2009), about the love of the poet John Keats. In 2014, she presided over the Cannes jury. For television, she created the crime series Top of the Lake (2013-2017), with Elisabeth Moss.

media.title: Jane Campion and Sofia Coppola on The Power of the Dog
media.text: At the 2021 New York Film Festival, the two directors talk about the process of adapting Thomas Savage's novel.

profile.content: After more than a decade without making a feature, Campion adapted Thomas Savage's novel in The Power of the Dog (2021), a psychological western about a cruel rancher, played by Benedict Cumberbatch, in 1920s Montana, shot in New Zealand. The film won the Silver Lion for best director in Venice and, in 2022, earned Campion the Oscar for best director. She was the third woman to win in the category, after Kathryn Bigelow and Chloé Zhao, and the first to be nominated twice. She was also made a Dame of the New Zealand Order of Merit.

awards: Palme d'Or for The Piano (1993) and for the short Peel (1986), the Oscar for best original screenplay for The Piano (1994), the Oscar for best director for The Power of the Dog (2022) and the Silver Lion in Venice (2021).

name: Walter Salles
quote: This award goes to a woman who, after a loss suffered during an authoritarian regime, decided not to bend and to resist.

profile.content: Walter Moreira Salles Júnior was born in Rio de Janeiro on April 12, 1956, the son of banker and diplomat Walter Moreira Salles. Because of his father's work, he spent much of his childhood and adolescence in France and the United States and returned to Brazil at 15, in the middle of the military dictatorship, under the Médici government. He studied film at the University of Southern California and began his career in the 1980s, directing documentaries for television. With his brother João Moreira Salles, also a documentary filmmaker, he founded the production company VideoFilmes.

media.title: Central Station (1998)
media.text: Fernanda Montenegro and Vinícius de Oliveira on Dora and Josué's journey through the sertão: the film that put the cinema of the Retomada on the world map.

profile.content: Salles made his fiction debut with Exposure (1991). In the mid-1990s, in a Brazil rebuilding its cinema after the end of Embrafilme, he co-directed Foreign Land (1996) with Daniela Thomas, in black and white, about young people who leave the country during the Collor Plan. Worldwide recognition came with Central do Brasil (Central Station, 1998): the story of a letter writer at Rio's Central do Brasil station who accompanies a boy searching for his father in the Northeast won the Golden Bear in Berlin, the best actress award for Fernanda Montenegro and the Golden Globe, and was nominated for two Oscars. Then came Abril Despedaçado (Behind the Sun, 2001), with Rodrigo Santoro, adapted from the novel by Albanian writer Ismail Kadare.

In Diarios de motocicleta (The Motorcycle Diaries, 2004), Salles filmed in Spanish the journey of the young Ernesto Guevara across South America, before he became Che. The film was a success in Latin America and Europe and won the Oscar for best original song. Next came the American horror film Dark Water (2005) and Linha de Passe (2008), about four brothers from the outskirts of São Paulo, which won Sandra Corveloni the best actress award at Cannes. In 2012, he adapted Jack Kerouac's Beat Generation classic in On the Road (2012) and then spent more than a decade away from fiction features.

media.title: Walter Salles explains a scene from Central Station
media.text: The director explains how he built one of the film's most memorable sequences with Fernanda Montenegro.

profile.content: Salles returned in 2024 with Ainda Estou Aqui (I'm Still Here, 2024), adapted from Marcelo Rubens Paiva's book about his mother, Eunice, who stood up to the dictatorship after the disappearance of her husband, former congressman Rubens Paiva, in 1971. The film won the screenplay award in Venice, drew more than 5 million viewers to Brazilian theaters and won Fernanda Torres the Golden Globe for best actress. In March 2025, it became the first Brazilian film to win the Oscar for best international feature and was also nominated for best picture and best actress. Salles dedicated the award to Eunice and to the two Fernandas, Torres and Montenegro, who played her.

awards: Oscar for best international feature for I'm Still Here (2025), the Golden Bear and the Golden Globe for Central Station (1998-1999), the screenplay award in Venice (2024) and 2 BAFTAs for film not in the English language.

name: Spike Lee
quote: Let's make the moral choice between love and hate. Let's do the right thing!

profile.content: Shelton Jackson Lee was born in Atlanta on March 20, 1957, the son of a Black teacher of art and literature and jazz musician Bill Lee, and grew up in the Brooklyn neighborhood of New York. His mother gave him the nickname Spike. He studied communications at Morehouse College, a historically Black university in Atlanta, and then film at New York University (NYU). His thesis film, Joe's Bed-Stuy Barbershop: We Cut Heads (1983), with a score by his father and cinematography by his classmate Ernest Dickerson, won a Student Academy Award.

media.title: Do the Right Thing (1989)
media.text: The hottest day of summer on a Brooklyn street, where racial tension builds until it explodes: Spike Lee's most important film.

profile.content: Made for US$ 175,000, shot in two weeks and in black and white, She's Gotta Have It (1986) grossed more than US$ 7 million and helped pave the way for American independent cinema in the 1980s. Lee wrote, produced, directed, edited and acted in the film, released by his production company, 40 Acres and a Mule. In 1989 came Do the Right Thing (1989), about a hot day in Brooklyn that ends in police violence and a riot. The film was nominated for the Oscar for screenplay but left out of the best picture and director categories, an omission still remembered as an injustice.

In the 1990s, Lee filmed Black American life in all its facets: jazz in Mo' Better Blues (1990), interracial romance in Jungle Fever (1991) and, above all, the biopic Malcolm X (1992), with Denzel Washington, which he fought to make his way, even turning to donations from Black celebrities to finish the film. He also made documentaries, such as 4 Little Girls, about the racist bombing of a church in Alabama, and the satire Bamboozled (2000). After 9/11, he filmed New York in 25th Hour (2002).

media.title: How Spike Lee shoots films at three different budgets
media.text: The In Depth Cine channel compares the cinematography of Spike Lee's low-budget and big-budget films, including the famous shot in which the actor seems to float down the street.

profile.content: The thriller Inside Man (2006) was the biggest commercial success of his career. In 2015, Lee received an honorary Oscar and, three years later, released BlacKkKlansman (2018), the true story of a Black police officer who infiltrated the Ku Klux Klan. The film won the Grand Prix at Cannes and gave Lee his first competitive Oscar, for adapted screenplay. Then came Da 5 Bloods (2020), about Black veterans of the Vietnam War, and Highest 2 Lowest (2025), a reinterpretation of Akira Kurosawa's High and Low, with Denzel Washington. A die-hard fan of the New York Knicks, he is a fixture courtside.

awards: Honorary Oscar (2015), the Oscar for best adapted screenplay for BlacKkKlansman (2019), the Grand Prix at Cannes (2018) and the US National Medal of Arts (2023).

name: Wong Kar-wai
quote: He remembers those vanished years as though looking through a dusty window pane: the past is something he could see, but not touch.

profile.content: Wong Kar-wai was born in Shanghai on July 17, 1958, the youngest of three children, the son of a sailor. At five, he moved with his parents to Hong Kong, while his older siblings stayed in China. Unable to speak Cantonese, he spent his afternoons at the movies with his mother: "The only hobby I had as a child was watching movies," he said. He studied graphic design at the Hong Kong Polytechnic, but dropped out to join a training program at the TV station TVB. In the 1980s, he wrote scripts for soap operas and commercial films.

media.title: In the Mood for Love (2000)
media.text: Maggie Cheung and Tony Leung in In the Mood for Love: Wong's most celebrated film, about a love that is never fulfilled.

profile.content: Wong made his directing debut with the crime film As Tears Go By (1988), a hit in Hong Kong. But he preferred a personal path: Days of Being Wild (1990) traded action for mood and feelings and flopped at the box office, although it is now considered a classic. In 1992, he founded the production company Jet Tone. While editing the martial arts epic Ashes of Time (1994), he made Chungking Express (1994) in a few months, two stories of lonely policemen in love, shot with a handheld camera by cinematographer Christopher Doyle. Quentin Tarantino fell in love with the film and helped release it in the United States.

Fallen Angels (1995) took the universe of Chungking Express into the night and the neon. In Happy Together (1997), Tony Leung and Leslie Cheung play a gay couple in crisis in Buenos Aires, on the eve of Hong Kong's handover to China. The film won Wong the Best Director award at Cannes. In 2000 came In the Mood for Love (2000), shot over 15 months, with more than 30 times the footage that made it into the final cut. Maggie Cheung's dresses, the score and the slow motion made it one of the most beautiful and most imitated films of the century.

media.title: The world of Wong Kar-wai
media.text: A BFI video essay on the themes, music and images that recur from film to film in the director's work.

profile.content: Wong took four years to finish 2046 (2004), a follow-up to In the Mood for Love with science fiction elements, and then made his only English-language film, My Blueberry Nights (2007), with singer Norah Jones. In 2006, he was the first Chinese director to preside over the Cannes jury. His next film, The Grandmaster (2013), about kung fu master Ip Man, came out in 2013. In 2021, he released restored versions of all his films and, between 2023 and 2024, directed the series Blossoms Shanghai, set in his hometown in the 1990s.

awards: Best Director award at Cannes for Happy Together (1997), the first given to a Chinese director. He presided over the Cannes Film Festival jury in 2006.

name: Alfonso Cuarón
quote: As artists, our job is to look where others don't.

profile.content: Alfonso Cuarón Orozco was born in Mexico City on November 28, 1961. He studied philosophy at the National Autonomous University of Mexico and film at the same university's film studies center, where he met cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, his partner for almost his entire career, but he was expelled from the program. He started in television as a technician and then as a director, and was an assistant director on several films. He made his feature debut with Sólo con tu pareja (1992), a comedy about a womanizer who believes he has contracted AIDS, a hit in Mexico that opened the doors of Hollywood to him.

media.title: Gravity (2013)
media.text: Sandra Bullock adrift in space: Gravity combined extremely long takes and digital effects to create the sensation of floating in orbit.

profile.content: In the United States, Cuarón directed A Little Princess (1995), a delicate adaptation of a children's classic, and Great Expectations (1998), a modern version of Charles Dickens. In 2001, he returned to Mexico to shoot Y tu mamá también (2001), with Gael García Bernal and Diego Luna, the road trip of two teenagers with an older woman that, between the lines, portrays the country's inequality. Its success led him to direct Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004), considered by many fans the most beautiful film in the series. With his friends and fellow Mexicans Guillermo del Toro and Alejandro González Iñárritu, he formed the trio nicknamed the "Three Amigos" of new Mexican cinema.

Children of Men (2006), about a world where women can no longer get pregnant, became famous for its breathtaking long takes, shot with a handheld camera in the middle of battles. In Gravity (2013), Sandra Bullock and George Clooney are left adrift in space after an accident. The film grossed more than US$ 700 million and won seven Oscars, including best director, which made Cuarón the first Latin American to win in the category. In 2015, he presided over the Venice Film Festival jury.

media.title: Alfonso Cuarón's long take
media.text: The Royal Ocean Film Society channel analyzes how Cuarón builds his long scenes without cuts, from Y Tu Mamá También to Gravity.
media.source: YouTube: The Royal Ocean Film Society channel

profile.content: In Roma (2018), Cuarón returned to his childhood in 1970s Mexico City through the story of the family's maid, played by newcomer Yalitza Aparicio, of Indigenous descent. Shot in black and white and photographed by the director himself, the film won the Golden Lion in Venice and was released by Netflix. At the Oscars, it won for director, cinematography and foreign language film, Mexico's first. In 2024, Cuarón wrote and directed every episode of the series Disclaimer, with Cate Blanchett, for Apple TV+.

awards: 4 Oscars (director and editing for Gravity; director and cinematography for Roma, which also won best foreign language film) and the Golden Lion for Roma (2018).

name: Guillermo del Toro
quote: The greatest thing our art does is erase the lines in the sand.

profile.content: Guillermo del Toro Gómez was born in Guadalajara, Mexico, on October 9, 1964, the son of a businessman in the car trade. Raised in a Catholic environment that he himself describes as "morbid", he fell in love early with monsters, comics and horror films. As a teenager, he made shorts in Super 8 and even built sets and a hundred puppets for an animated film he never finished. He studied makeup and special effects with the American Dick Smith, of The Exorcist, worked for ten years in the field with his own company and helped found the Guadalajara Film Festival.

media.title: Pan's Labyrinth (2006)
media.text: In Franco's Spain, the girl Ofelia finds a faun in a labyrinth: the dark fairy tale that won three Oscars.

profile.content: His first feature, Cronos (1993), about an antiques dealer who finds an artifact that grants eternal life, won an award at the Cannes Critics' Week. His Hollywood debut, Mimic (1997), was a bitter experience, with constant studio interference. In 1997, his father was kidnapped in Guadalajara, and his friend James Cameron helped the family pay the ransom. Shaken, del Toro returned to Spanish with El espinazo del diablo (The Devil's Backbone, 2001), a ghost story set in the Spanish Civil War, and alternated with American hits such as Blade II (2002) and Hellboy (2004), always with monsters treated with more empathy than humans.

El laberinto del fauno (Pan's Labyrinth, 2006) blended fairy tale and historical horror in Franco's Spain and won three Oscars (cinematography, art direction and makeup), as well as competing for best foreign language film. With his friends Alfonso Cuarón and Alejandro González Iñárritu, del Toro formed the trio known as the "Three Amigos" of Mexican cinema. After leaving the director's chair of The Hobbit during pre-production, he made Pacific Rim (2013), with giant robots fighting monsters, and the gothic romance Crimson Peak (2015). He also created animated and horror series for television.

media.title: How Guillermo del Toro deals with trauma
media.text: The Storytellers video essay shows how fantasy and monsters serve to confront war, loss and violence in the director's films.

profile.content: The Shape of Water (2017), the love story between a mute cleaning woman and an amphibian creature in Cold War America, won the Golden Lion and four Oscars, including best picture and director. Then came the noir Nightmare Alley (2021) and the stop-motion Guillermo del Toro's Pinocchio (2022), winner of the Oscar for animated feature. In 2025, he fulfilled his dream of adapting Mary Shelley's novel in Frankenstein (2025), with Oscar Isaac and Jacob Elordi, released by Netflix. The film competed in Venice, received nine Oscar nominations, including best picture, and won for production design, costume design and makeup.

media.quote: This movie closes a cycle. If you look at the lineage, from Cronos to The Devil's Backbone, to Pan's Labyrinth, it's the evolution of an aesthetic and of an empathy.
media.author: Guillermo del Toro on Frankenstein (2023)

awards: 3 Oscars (best picture and director for The Shape of Water and animated feature for Pinocchio) and the Golden Lion for The Shape of Water (2017). Frankenstein (2025) received 9 Oscar nominations and won 3.

name: Denis Villeneuve
quote: Frankly, I hate dialogue. Dialogue is for theater and television.

profile.content: Denis Villeneuve was born on October 3, 1967, in Gentilly, a small town on the banks of the St. Lawrence River, in the Canadian province of Quebec. He studied at a seminary in Trois-Rivières, then science and, finally, film at the Université du Québec à Montréal. A passionate reader of science fiction, he says he had dreamed of adapting Frank Herbert's Dune since he was a teenager. He started his career making shorts and, in 1991, won a young filmmakers' competition run by the public broadcaster Radio-Canada, which took him filming in several countries.

media.title: Dune (2021)
media.text: Paul Atreides in the desert of Arrakis: Villeneuve brought some 40 years of fascination with the book to the scale of IMAX.

profile.content: Villeneuve made his feature debut with August 32nd on Earth (1998), screened in the Un Certain Regard section at Cannes, and followed it with Maelström (2000), awarded at the Toronto Film Festival. After a break to "recenter his life", he returned with Polytechnique (2009), in black and white, about the massacre of 14 women at the École Polytechnique in Montreal in 1989. In 2010, Incendies (2010), adapted from Wajdi Mouawad's play, followed twins searching for their mother's past in the Middle East and was nominated for the Oscar for best foreign language film. Hollywood began to compete for him.

In English, Villeneuve made a string of dark thrillers: Prisoners (2013), about a father who kidnaps the suspect in his daughter's disappearance; Enemy (2014), with Jake Gyllenhaal; and Sicario (2015), about the drug war on the Mexican border, which competed for the Palme d'Or. Arrival (2016), with Amy Adams as a linguist trying to communicate with aliens, received eight Oscar nominations, including best director. In 2017, he took on the challenge of continuing a Ridley Scott classic in Blade Runner 2049 (2017), acclaimed by critics but below expectations at the box office.

media.title: Denis Villeneuve interviewed by Christopher Nolan
media.text: A conversation between two of today's greatest directors of spectacle cinema about the making of Dune: Part Two.

profile.content: Villeneuve finally adapted Dune (2021), released in 2021 in the middle of the pandemic, and won six Oscars. The sequel, Dune: Part Two (2024), grossed more than US$ 700 million in 2024 and became the biggest hit of his career. The third part, based on Dune Messiah, began shooting in 2025 and is set for release on December 18, 2026. In June 2025, the studio Amazon MGM announced that Villeneuve will direct the next James Bond film, scheduled for 2028.

media.quote: To me, he is sacred territory. I intend to honor the tradition and open the way for many new missions to come.
media.author: Denis Villeneuve on being announced as director of the new James Bond (2025)

awards: Nominated for the Oscar for best director for Arrival (2017). Dune (2021) won 6 Oscars and Dune: Part Two (2024) 2 more. Incendies (2010) was nominated for the Oscar for best foreign language film.

name: Kleber Mendonça Filho
quote: If you go, go in peace.

profile.content: Kleber de Mendonça Vasconcellos Filho was born in Recife on November 22, 1968, the son of a historian. Between the ages of 13 and 18, he lived in Colchester, England, where his mother was doing her doctorate. Back in Brazil, he graduated in journalism from the Federal University of Pernambuco and built a long career as a film critic, writing for newspapers and magazines and for his website, CinemaScópio, a name he would later give to his production company. For years he was also the film programmer of the Joaquim Nabuco Foundation in Recife, and he began filming with experimental videos in the 1990s.

media.title: Bacurau (2019)
media.text: A village in the sertão that vanishes from the map and comes under attack by foreigners: the western by Kleber and Juliano Dornelles won the Jury Prize at Cannes.

profile.content: In the 2000s, Kleber made award-winning shorts that already announced the themes of his work, such as Green Vinyl (2004) and the mockumentary Cold Tropics (2009), about a climate change that freezes the city. His first feature was the documentary Critic (2008), with interviews with critics and filmmakers. His fiction debut, Neighboring Sounds (2012), portrays a middle-class street in Recife that hires a private security company and uses sound to reveal the class tensions inherited from slavery. Critic A. O. Scott of The New York Times included it among the ten best films of 2012.

In Aquarius (2016), Sônia Braga plays Clara, a retired music critic who refuses to sell her apartment to a construction company. At the Cannes premiere, the cast and crew protested on the red carpet against the impeachment proceedings against Dilma Rousseff, which caused great controversy in Brazil. Co-directed with Juliano Dornelles, Bacurau (2019) shared the Jury Prize at Cannes with Les Misérables and became a box-office hit. In Pictures of Ghosts (2023), Kleber returned to documentary to tell the story of the street cinemas of downtown Recife and of the apartment where he lived.

media.title: Kleber Mendonça Filho and the films that inspired The Secret Agent
media.text: In a Film at Lincoln Center video, the director discusses the 1970s Brazilian and international cinema references behind the film.

profile.content: O Agente Secreto (The Secret Agent, 2025) is a political thriller set in Recife in 1977, at the height of the dictatorship, with Wagner Moura as a technology expert trying to escape a violent past. At Cannes in 2025, Kleber won the Best Director award and Moura won best actor. In January 2026, the film won the Golden Globes for best non-English language film and best actor in a drama and then received four Oscar nominations: best picture, international feature, actor and casting. It was one of the greatest moments in the history of Brazilian cinema, a year after the Oscar for I'm Still Here.

media.quote: One of the best films made anywhere in the world recently.
media.author: Caetano Veloso on Neighboring Sounds, in his column in the newspaper O Globo

awards: Best Director award at Cannes for The Secret Agent (2025), 2 Golden Globes and 4 Oscar nominations for the same film, and the Jury Prize at Cannes for Bacurau (2019).

Kleber Mendonça Filho and Emilie Lesclaux on The Secret Agent

name: Bong Joon-ho
quote: Once you overcome the one-inch-tall barrier of subtitles, you will be introduced to so many more amazing films.

profile.content: Bong Joon-ho was born in Daegu, South Korea, on September 14, 1969, the youngest of four children. His father was a graphic designer and art teacher. While he was still a child, the family moved to Seoul, near the Han River, which would be the setting of one of his films. He watched many films on TV, among them Black Orpheus, shot in Rio de Janeiro, which made a strong impression on him. In 1988, he entered Yonsei University to study sociology, at a time of intense student mobilization for democracy. He then attended the Korean Academy of Film Arts, where he made 16 mm shorts screened at festivals.

media.title: Parasite (2019)
media.text: The Kim family infiltrates the home of the wealthy Parks: the satire on inequality was the first non-English language film to win the Oscar for best picture.

profile.content: His first feature, Barking Dogs Never Bite (2000), a black comedy, was not a success but became a cult film. Recognition came with Memories of Murder (2003), based on a real serial killer case in rural Korea in the 1980s, one of the country's most celebrated films. In The Host (2006), a monster emerges from the Han River and attacks Seoul: the film broke South Korea's box-office record. Next, he made Mother (2009), about a mother trying to prove the innocence of her son, accused of murder. Bong became known for his abrupt shifts in tone, which go from drama to slapstick in the same scene.

Bong made his English-language debut with Snowpiercer (2013), adapted from a French graphic novel, about a train where the survivors of a new ice age live divided by class, from the luxury car to the back of the train. In 2017, Okja (2017), about a girl and a super-pig bred by a multinational, was produced by Netflix and caused controversy when it was screened in competition at Cannes without a theatrical release in France. Social inequality, present in almost all his films, would take its most perfect form in his next work.

media.title: Parasite: Bong Joon-ho's mastery of genre and tone
media.text: The StudioBinder channel analyzes how Parasite moves from comedy to thriller to horror without losing control.

profile.content: Parasite (2019) won the Palme d'Or, the first for a Korean film, and four Oscars in February 2020, including best picture, the first for a non-English language production. On receiving the award for best director, Bong cited Martin Scorsese, who was in the audience, as an inspiration. In 2021, he presided over the Venice jury. He then returned to English with Mickey 17 (2025), with Robert Pattinson as an expendable worker who is cloned every time he dies, released at the 2025 Berlin Film Festival. He is also preparing an animated film about deep-sea creatures.

media.quote: The most personal is the most creative.
media.author: Bong Joon-ho quoting Martin Scorsese at the Oscars (2020)

awards: Palme d'Or (2019) and 4 Oscars (best picture, director, original screenplay and international feature) for Parasite. He presided over the Venice Film Festival jury in 2021.

name: Céline Sciamma
quote: Cinema is always political.

profile.content: Céline Sciamma was born on November 12, 1978, and grew up in Cergy-Pontoise, on the outskirts of Paris. A voracious reader as a child, she discovered cinema as a teenager, influenced by her grandmother, a fan of Hollywood classics, and went to the town's art house cinema three times a week. She earned a master's degree in French literature at the University of Nanterre and then studied screenwriting at La Fémis, France's leading film school, between 2001 and 2005. The screenplay she submitted as her graduation project would become her first feature, which she did not even intend to direct.

image.content_description: Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019)

media.title: Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019)
media.text: A painter and the young woman she is portraying on an island in 18th-century Brittany: the film became a manifesto of the female gaze in cinema.

profile.content: In Naissance des pieuvres (Water Lilies, 2007), shot in Cergy, Sciamma used synchronized swimming to talk about the awakening of desire among teenagers. Tomboy (2011), written in three weeks and shot in 20 days, follows a ten-year-old child who introduces themselves to new friends as a boy; it won the Teddy Award in Berlin and was screened in French schools. In Bande de filles (Girlhood, 2014), a young Black woman from the outskirts of Paris drops out of school and joins a girl gang. The director considers the three films a trilogy about coming of age, almost always with non-professional actors.

Sciamma also began writing for other directors: she wrote the stop-motion animated film My Life as a Zucchini (2016), nominated for an Oscar, and worked with André Téchiné. In 2019, she released Portrait de la jeune fille en feu (Portrait of a Lady on Fire, 2019), with Adèle Haenel and Noémie Merlant, about the love between a painter and the woman she must portray for an arranged marriage. The film won the screenplay award and the Queer Palm at Cannes and is today one of the most celebrated French films of the century. Sciamma is one of the founders of the 50/50 movement, which fights for gender equality in French cinema.

media.title: Céline Sciamma in BAFTA's screenwriters lecture series
media.text: The director talks about how she writes, the female gaze and the making of Portrait of a Lady on Fire.

profile.content: Shot during the pandemic, Petite Maman (2021) follows an eight-year-old girl who, after her grandmother's death, meets a girl of the same age in the woods who is, in fact, her mother as a child. It premiered in Berlin in 2021 and won the audience award in San Sebastián. That same year, Sciamma co-wrote Jacques Audiard's Paris, 13th District. In 2026, the French distributor MK2 acquired the rights to her entire filmography, and a new version of Tomboy was screened in Berlin, where she received an honorary Teddy.

media.quote: Our stories are powerful because they are dangerous. We are dangerous.
media.author: Céline Sciamma on the male gaze in cinema

awards: Best Screenplay and the Queer Palm at Cannes for Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019), the Teddy Award in Berlin for Tomboy (2011) and an honorary Teddy (2026).

name: Justine Triet
quote: When we lack an element to judge something, and that lack is unbearable, all we can do is decide.

profile.content: Justine Triet was born on July 17, 1978, in Fécamp, Normandy, and grew up in Paris with two siblings, spending much of her childhood in a Buddhist community. She graduated from the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. She began by making short documentaries on political and social issues: Sur Place (2007) filmed the 2006 student protests in France with more nuance than television showed, and Solférino (2009) followed the 2007 French presidential election. She shot, directed and edited her work on her own.

media.title: Anatomy of a Fall (2023)
media.text: Sandra Hüller as a writer accused of her husband's death: the trial exposes, scene by scene, a marriage in pieces.

profile.content: In 2012, Triet moved into fiction with the short Two Ships, awarded in Berlin. Her first feature, La Bataille de Solférino (Age of Panic, 2013), mixes a couple's fight with the live coverage of the night of François Hollande's election in 2012, and made the best-of-the-year list of Cahiers du Cinéma. Then came the comedy Victoria (In Bed with Victoria, 2016), with Virginie Efira as a lawyer in crisis, nominated for the César for best film, and Sibyl (2019), also with Efira, which competed for the Palme d'Or. Her partner, filmmaker Arthur Harari, collaborated on some of her screenplays.

Written with Harari, Anatomie d'une chute (Anatomy of a Fall, 2023) follows the trial of a German writer accused of killing her husband in the French Alps, while the couple's blind son tries to understand what happened. The film won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, and Triet became the third woman to receive the award. She then won two Golden Globes and, in 2024, five Oscar nominations. Triet was the first Frenchwoman nominated for the Oscar for best director and won, with Harari, the award for best original screenplay. The dog Messi, who plays Snoop in the film, also became a celebrity during awards season.

media.title: Justine Triet on Anatomy of a Fall and the Palme d'Or
media.text: In an interview with the Canadian program Q, the director talks about the writing process for the film and the future of French cinema.

profile.content: On receiving the Palme d'Or, Triet criticized Emmanuel Macron's government for its crackdown on protests against the pension reform and for the commercialization of culture, which drew harsh reactions from ministers. She dedicated the award to young directors and to those who struggle to make films. She is part of the 50/50 collective, which advocates gender equality in French cinema, and in 2024 she was invited to join the Hollywood Academy. Among her influences, she lists filmmakers as different as Gus Van Sant, Robert Zemeckis and documentary maker Frederick Wiseman.

awards: Palme d'Or (2023), the Oscar and BAFTA for best original screenplay and 2 Golden Globes (screenplay and non-English language film) for Anatomy of a Fall.

name: Ryusuke Hamaguchi
quote: To a certain extent, every film is fiction and documentary at the same time.

profile.content: Ryusuke Hamaguchi was born in Kawasaki, Japan, on December 16, 1978, the son of an employee of the Ministry of Construction, and spent part of his childhood in Iran because of his father's work. He entered the University of Tokyo with no special interest in film, but fell in love with movies at the university film club, where he shot 8 mm shorts. After graduating, he worked for a few years in the commercial industry and then entered the film master's program at the Tokyo University of the Arts, where he studied under director Kiyoshi Kurosawa.

media.title: Drive My Car (2021)
media.text: A theater director and the driver who takes him along the roads of Hiroshima: the three-hour film was the first Japanese film nominated for the Oscar for best picture.

profile.content: Hamaguchi's graduation film, Passion (2008), was selected for the Tokyo Filmex festival. After the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, he co-directed with Kō Sakai a trilogy of documentaries with survivors of the tragedy, which taught him to listen to people speak. Recognition came with Happy Hour (2015), a drama of more than five hours about four friends from Kobe, created from workshops with amateur actresses. The film competed at the Locarno Film Festival in 2015, where the four leads shared the best actress award.

Asako I & II (2018) took Hamaguchi to the Cannes competition for the first time. In 2021, he released two acclaimed films. Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy (2021), three stories about chance and coincidence, won the Grand Jury Prize in Berlin. Drive My Car (2021), adapted from a short story by Haruki Murakami, follows a grieving actor and theater director who stages Chekhov's Uncle Vanya with actors who speak different languages. The film won the screenplay award at Cannes and the Golden Globe.

media.title: Drive My Car and intertextuality
media.text: The Accented Cinema channel shows how Hamaguchi interweaves Murakami, Chekhov and the lives of the characters.

profile.content: At the 2022 Oscars, Drive My Car won the award for best international feature and was the first Japanese film nominated for best picture. Hamaguchi was also nominated as director and screenwriter. He then made Evil Does Not Exist (2023), about a village threatened by a tourism project, which won the Grand Jury Prize in Venice in 2023. His first French-language film, All of a Sudden (2026), with Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto, premiered in competition at Cannes in 2026, where the two shared the best actress award.

media.quote: What the camera captures is a documentary about the actors, because they are doing something that happens only once.
media.author: Ryusuke Hamaguchi

awards: Oscar for best international feature and the Golden Globe for Drive My Car (2022), Best Screenplay at Cannes (2021) and the Grand Jury Prize in Berlin (2021) and in Venice (2023).

name: Jordan Peele
quote: The Sunken Place means we're marginalized. No matter how hard we scream, the system silences us.

profile.content: Jordan Haworth Peele was born in New York on February 21, 1979, the son of a white mother and a Black father whom he last saw when he was seven. He was raised by his mother on Manhattan's Upper West Side and grew up fascinated by horror films, which he watched in secret. He studied at Sarah Lawrence College but dropped out to do improv comedy with groups such as The Second City in Chicago. In 2003, he joined the cast of the comedy show Mad TV, where he stayed for five seasons and met his partner Keegan-Michael Key.

media.title: Get Out (2017)
media.text: Daniel Kaluuya paralyzed in the "Sunken Place": Get Out turned the disguised racism of white liberals into a horror film.

profile.content: With Key, Peele created the sketch show Key & Peele (2012-2015), which went viral online with jokes about race, identity and pop culture and won an Emmy and a Peabody Award. One of the duo's most famous impressions was of then-president Barack Obama and his "anger translator". In the same year the series premiered, Peele founded the production company Monkeypaw, named after a horror story. While succeeding in comedy, he was secretly writing a screenplay about a young Black man who visits his white girlfriend's family.

Get Out (2017) cost US$ 4.5 million and grossed more than US$ 255 million, becoming one of the most profitable horror films in history. Critics hailed it as a masterpiece. At the Oscars, it received four nominations, including best picture and director, and gave Peele the award for best original screenplay: it was the first time a Black screenwriter had won in the category. That same year, he was one of the producers of Spike Lee's BlacKkKlansman, also nominated for best picture. Peele announced that he intended to give up acting to focus on directing.

media.title: Jordan Peele breaks down fan theories about Get Out
media.text: In a Vanity Fair video, the director discusses the film's hidden symbols and details that viewers have discovered.

profile.content: In Us (2019), Lupita Nyong'o faces a family of identical doubles who emerge from the tunnels beneath the United States. In Nope (2022), a science fiction western shot with IMAX cameras, two siblings who train horses for Hollywood try to film a flying saucer. Through Monkeypaw, he also produced and co-wrote Candyman (2021) and the animated film Wendell & Wild (2022). His fourth film as director was once scheduled for release in October 2026, but it was taken off the studio's calendar in 2025 and remains undated.

awards: Oscar for best original screenplay for Get Out (2018), the first for a Black screenwriter in the category, and nominations for best picture and director.

name: Chloé Zhao
quote: I have always found goodness in the people I met, everywhere I went in the world.

profile.content: Chloé Zhao, born Zhao Ting, came into the world in Beijing on March 31, 1982, the daughter of an executive at a large Chinese state-owned steel company. A rebellious student, she preferred drawing manga-style comics and writing stories to studying, and said she was marked by Wong Kar-wai's Happy Together. At 15, she was sent to a boarding school in England and later moved on her own to Los Angeles. She graduated in political science from Mount Holyoke College, worked as a bartender and, in 2010, entered New York University's graduate film program, where Spike Lee was one of her teachers.

media.title: Nomadland (2020)
media.text: Frances McDormand as a widow who lives in a van across the American West: the film features real nomads playing themselves.

profile.content: Zhao made her debut with Songs My Brothers Taught Me (2015), shot on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation in South Dakota, about two Lakota siblings, screened at Sundance and at the Directors' Fortnight in Cannes. In The Rider (2018), she returned to the same region to tell the true story of a young rodeo rider barred from riding after an accident, played by himself. The film won an award at Cannes and showed the director's method: non-professional actors, natural light and vast landscapes of the American heartland.

In Nomadland (2021), Frances McDormand plays a woman who loses everything in the 2008 crisis and starts living on the road, working seasonal jobs, alongside real nomads. The film won the Golden Lion in Venice, the People's Choice Award in Toronto and, in 2021, the Oscars for best picture, director and actress. Zhao was the second woman to win the Oscar for best director, after Kathryn Bigelow, and the first woman of color. That same year, she released Eternals (2021), a Marvel superhero film that received a cool reception from critics.

media.title: Why Nomadland won the Oscar for best director
media.text: Thomas Flight's video essay analyzes the camera, the light and the blend of documentary and fiction in Chloé Zhao's film.

profile.content: Zhao adapted Maggie O'Farrell's novel in Hamnet (2025), with Jessie Buckley and Paul Mescal, about the grief of Agnes and William Shakespeare over the death of their son, Hamnet. The film premiered in 2025 and won the People's Choice Award in Toronto, Zhao's second, the Golden Globe for best drama and the BAFTA for outstanding British film. At the 2026 Oscars, it received eight nominations, including best picture and director, which made Zhao the second woman nominated twice as director, and won Jessie Buckley the award for best actress.

awards: Oscars for best picture and director for Nomadland (2021), the Golden Lion (2020) and the Golden Globe for best motion picture drama for Hamnet (2026). Two-time winner of the People's Choice Award in Toronto.

name: Greta Gerwig
quote: Women have minds and souls, as well as just hearts.

profile.content: Greta Celeste Gerwig was born in Sacramento, California, on August 4, 1983, the daughter of a nurse and a credit union employee. She attended an all-girls Catholic school, danced, fenced and wanted to be a playwright. At Barnard College in New York, she was turned down by the playwriting graduate programs and ended up acting in very low-budget films of the so-called mumblecore movement, with improvised dialogue and handheld cameras. With Joe Swanberg, she co-directed Nights and Weekends (2008). In 2010, she drew attention as an actress in Noah Baumbach's Greenberg.

media.title: Lady Bird (2017)
media.text: Saoirse Ronan as a teenager who wants to get out of Sacramento: Gerwig's love letter to the city where she grew up.

profile.content: With Baumbach, who would become her husband, Gerwig wrote and starred in Frances Ha (2012), about an aimless 27-year-old dancer in New York, which earned her a Golden Globe nomination for best actress. Her solo directing debut came in 2017 with Lady Bird (2017), inspired by her own adolescence. The film won the Golden Globe for best comedy and five Oscar nominations. Gerwig was the fifth woman in history nominated for the Oscar for best director. It was proof that her intimate stories about mothers, daughters and small towns could win over a wide audience.

In Little Women (2019), Gerwig reinvented Louisa May Alcott's classic, with Saoirse Ronan, Florence Pugh, Emma Watson and Timothée Chalamet. She shuffled the book's chronology and turned the story into a commentary on female authorship and money: at the end, Jo fights for the rights to her own novel. The film received six Oscar nominations, including adapted screenplay for the director, and won for costume design. Gerwig came to be seen as one of the most important voices of Hollywood's new generation.

media.title: Why Greta Gerwig's Little Women is the best one
media.text: Thomas Flight's video essay analyzes how the nonlinear editing transforms Louisa May Alcott's novel.

profile.content: Barbie (2023), written with Baumbach and starring Margot Robbie and Ryan Gosling, became a phenomenon in July 2023, in the so-called "Barbenheimer", opening on the same day as Oppenheimer. It was the first film directed solely by a woman to pass US$ 1 billion at the box office and the highest-grossing film of the year worldwide. In 2024, Gerwig presided over the Cannes jury, the first American woman director in the role. Her next film is Narnia: The Magician's Nephew, for Netflix, scheduled for release in IMAX theaters in November 2026 before arriving on streaming.

awards: Nominated for 4 Oscars as director and screenwriter (Lady Bird, Little Women and Barbie). Golden Globe for best comedy for Lady Bird and president of the Cannes Film Festival jury (2024).
